name: ChargeFile
one_liner: Turns a small hospital's own chargemaster export, payer-contract terms and an 835 remittance extract into the CMS v3.0 standard-charges machine-readable file — validator-clean, attestation block populated, named to CMS's convention — plus the cms-hpt.txt, regenerated every time CMS moves the schema.
artifact: The exact artifact is the file CMS names in regulation: `<ein>_<hospital-name>_standardcharges.json` (or the CSV 'tall'/'wide' equivalents), conforming to CMS's V3.0.0 JSON schema, together with the required `cms-hpt.txt` at the web root and a dated pass report from CMS's own validator. Spec: V3.0.0_Hospital_price_transparency_schema.json (fetched 2026-08-20, HTTP 200, 13,217 bytes) — root required properties hospital_name, standard_charge_information, last_updated_on, location_name, hospital_address, type_2_npi, license_information, attestation, version; per-payer properties standard_charge_dollar / standard_charge_percentage / standard_charge_algorithm plus the CY2026 additions median_amount, 10th_percentile, 90th_percentile, count, and attestation/attester_name/confirm_attestation. Submission cadence: 45 CFR 180.50(b)(3) — 'The hospital must update the standard charge information ... at least once annually' — plus a forced regeneration each time CMS revises the template (v2.0 → v2.1 → v2.2 → v3.0; the CMS validator library shipped 2.2.0 on 2026-02-09, 2.3.0 on 2026-04-08, 2.4.0 on 2026-04-28, 2.5.0 on 2026-06-02, 2.6.0 on 2026-08-18). Channel: the hospital is not filing to a portal — it must publish the file on a public website free of charge, without login, digitally searchable and directly downloadable (45 CFR 180.50(d)). ChargeFile emits the file for download and optionally hosts it at a stable URL the hospital links from its own site.
mandate: 45 CFR 180.50, fetched today 2026-08-20 via the eCFR versioner API (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-01/title-45.xml?part=180&subpart=B). Who must file: every hospital operating in the United States as defined at 45 CFR 180.20, explicitly including Critical Access Hospitals and Rural Emergency Hospitals. What: a single machine-readable file of all standard charges — gross charge, discounted cash price, payer-specific negotiated charge (dollar, percentage or algorithm), de-identified minimum and maximum — with billing codes, setting, modifiers, drug unit/type of measurement, hospital name/address/licence, and Type 2 NPI. Format: 'From July 1, 2024 forward, the hospital's machine-readable file must conform to a CMS template layout, data specifications, and data dictionary.' When: at least annually. New for 2026 (CMS repo README + CY2026 OPPS/ASC fact sheet, both fetched 2026-08-20): attestation statement, attester name, Type 2 NPI, median allowed amount, 10th percentile allowed amount, 90th percentile allowed amount and count of allowed amounts, all cited to 45 CFR 180.50(a)(3)(iii)-(iv) and (b)(2)(i)(A)/(b)(2)(ii)(C)(2), effective 1 January 2026 with CMS enforcement beginning 1 April 2026. The percentile fields have a published method, not a judgement: 'a lookback period of no less than 12 months and no longer than 15 months prior to posting the machine-readable file', sourced from 'electronic data interchange (EDI) 835 electronic remittance advice (ERA) or an alternative, equivalent source of remittance data', and where an exact percentile falls between observed values the hospital must 'use the next highest observed value'. Penalty: 45 CFR 180.90, fetched today — $300/day for hospitals with ≤30 beds, beds × $10/day for 31–550 beds, $5,500/day above 550 beds, CPI-adjusted annually. Enforcement is live: CMS imposed a CMP of $51,615.00 on Pinnacle Hospital, Crown Point IN, notice dated 3 June 2026 (UCN 2026HPT002), which I extracted from CMS's own redacted notice PDF today.
buyer: Small and rural hospitals with no revenue-integrity department: 1,382 Critical Access Hospitals, 43 Rural Emergency Hospitals, 624 Psychiatric hospitals and the small end of the 3,107 Acute Care Hospitals — counted today from CMS's own Hospital General Information CSV (data.cms.gov provider-data, dataset modified 2026-07-22, downloaded 2026-08-20, HTTP 200, 1,450,767 bytes, 5,419 rows; ownership split includes 512 'Government - Hospital District or Authority' and 393 'Government - Local'). Economic buyer is the CFO or the revenue-integrity/patient-financial-services manager — in a CAH usually the same person. Self-serve reachable because the product needs no EHR integration, no interface build and no IT project: every input is a file export those roles already produce (chargemaster extract, payer contract summary, 835 remittance). The same CMS dataset is the addressable-market list and the source of the hospital-identity fields the MRF header requires. Urgency is externally supplied and dated: 519 hospitals received noncompliance letters between April and early June 2026, spanning every state except Alaska (Texas 42, California 38, Indiana 34, Louisiana 27), and a warning letter is a 90-day clock followed by a 45-day corrective-action-plan clock.
input: Three customer-owned exports, all self-serve upload, no connectors, no credentials. (1) Chargemaster extract CSV: code, code type (CPT/HCPCS/DRG/NDC/APC/etc.), description, gross charge, discounted cash price, setting, modifiers, drug unit and type of measurement. (2) Payer/plan contract terms table: for each payer+plan, whether the negotiated charge is a dollar amount, a percentage of a named fee schedule, or an algorithm. (3) An 835 remittance extract covering a 12–15 month window. Friction is low on (1) and (2) — both are routine reports out of any patient-accounting system. (3) is the PHI trap and is designed out: 835 files carry patient names, member IDs and claim numbers, so ChargeFile parses the X12 835 in the customer's browser (WASM parser) and transmits only de-identified tuples of (payer, plan, billing code, modifier, allowed amount, service date bucket). No name, no member ID, no claim number, no date of birth ever reaches the server. The product states in-product that it is not a HIPAA business associate and holds no PHI, and the parser hard-fails rather than uploading if it encounters a field it cannot strip. That single design choice is also why fulfilment can be fully unattended: there is no BAA to negotiate per customer.
corpus: Every item below fetched today, 2026-08-20. (1) CMS v3.0 JSON schema — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CMSgov/hospital-price-transparency/master/documentation/JSON/schemas/V3.0.0_Hospital_price_transparency_schema.json — HTTP 200, 13,217 bytes, valid JSON Schema with conditional logic (e.g. if any payer entry carries standard_charge_dollar then minimum and maximum become required); property names confirmed by parsing: median_amount, 10th_percentile, 90th_percentile, count, attestation, attester_name, confirm_attestation, standard_charge_dollar/percentage/algorithm. (2) CMS data dictionaries and templates (CSV tall, CSV wide, JSON) in the same repo, master branch — README fetched today states v3.0 'effective January 1, 2026, with CMS enforcement beginning April 1, 2026' and enumerates each new data element against its CFR cite. Cadence: irregular, tied to annual OPPS/ASC rulemaking; liveness detected by SHA diff of the schema file. (3) CMS's own validator as an embeddable library — https://registry.npmjs.org/@cmsgov%2Fhpt-validator — latest 2.6.0 published 2026-08-18T21:07:45Z, licence CC0-1.0, with 2.2.0/2.3.0/2.4.0/2.5.0 published 2026-02-09 / 04-08 / 04-28 / 06-02. Two days old at time of writing: unambiguously alive, and public-domain so the generator can be gated on CMS's own pass/fail. (4) Medicare Physician Fee Schedule relative value files, needed to turn 'X% of Medicare' contract terms into the dollar amounts CMS's May-2025 guidance demands — https://www.cms.gov/files/zip/rvu26c-updated-06-30-2026.zip fetched HTTP 200, 6,160,522 bytes, containing PPRRVU2026_Jul_nonQPP.csv (2,622,166 bytes, internal date 2026-06-30), OPPSCAP_Jul.csv and GPCI2026.csv. Cadence quarterly (RVU26A/B/C/D); liveness detected from the dated filename. (5) CMS Hospital General Information CSV (identity fields + buyer universe), data.cms.gov provider-data metastore item xubh-q36u, modified 2026-07-22, download HTTP 200, 5,419 rows. (6) 45 CFR Part 180 text via the eCFR versioner API. Staleness handling: a cron diffs the schema SHA, the npm validator version and the RVU zip filename; if any moves, every customer file is flagged 'regenerate required — spec moved on <date>' rather than continuing to imply currency, and the product never asserts a file is compliant, only that it passed validator version N against schema version M on date D.
kill_checks: Pattern 1 — free first-party substitute. CMS ships tools, and I fetched them: an online Validator, a CLI validator, a MRF File Name Wizard (https://cmsgov.github.io/hpt-tool/filename-wizard/) and a TXT File Generator (https://cmsgov.github.io/hpt-tool/txt-generator/), plus blank CSV/JSON templates and a data dictionary in the GitHub repo. Every one of these validates, names or formats; not one of them generates the MRF from hospital data. This is exactly the permitted shape — the agency publishes the spec and a validator, not a generator. CMS does not compute the numbers either: 45 CFR 180.50(b)(2)(ii)(C)(2) puts the median/percentile computation on the hospital. SURVIVES. Pattern 2 — live micro-SaaS at a fraction of the imagined price. I hunted and fetched: Rivet Health pricing page (demo-gated, no dollar figures), Panacea machine-readable-files page (Request Demo, no prices, phone number), PMMC price-transparency page (Book a Demo, no prices), Payerset pricing page ('Rather than force-fit you into a tier, we scope a package to your use case' — and it is a data-access product, Rate Explorer + Data Lake, not an MRF generator), Turquoise Health for-providers page (enterprise framing, MRF *search*, no MRF creation offering, no prices). Searches across Product Hunt/indie/GitHub for a self-serve chargemaster→MRF generator returned only CMS's own repos. No published-price self-serve incumbent found. SURVIVES, with the honest caveat that the absence of any published price also means there is no anchor. Pattern 3 — bundled in software the buyer already pays for. This is the live risk and I chased it. Craneware's Trisus Pricing Transparency is genuinely free: I pulled the page text and it says 'Available at no cost to all US healthcare providers' and 'this offering is free to every U.S. healthcare provider owning or managing acute care hospitals', with a patient-facing hosted search site. But the same page text contains zero occurrences of 'machine-readable', 'machine readable', 'v3.0', 'allowed amount', 'percentile', 'attestation' or '2026' — it is a consumer-display and analytics product anchored on the 2021 rule, and its free hosting is scoped to acute-care hospital owners, which excludes much of the CAH/REH base. TruBridge's price-transparency product (BusinessWire launch) is likewise a patient estimator, not an MRF generator. Craneware Trisus Chargemaster is chargemaster management. So the artifact this product makes is not currently bundled — but the ingredients sit inside vendors who could bundle it, and I am naming that as the top risk rather than claiming it away. SURVIVES, CONDITIONALLY. Pattern 4 — premise misstated vs primary text. Checked against the primary text itself rather than commentary: 45 CFR 180.50 fetched from eCFR, 45 CFR 180.90 fetched from eCFR, the CY2026 OPPS/ASC HPT fact sheet fetched from cms.gov, and the CMS repo README which tabulates each new element against its CFR cite. The mandate, the annual cadence, the CMS-template conformance requirement and the 2026 additions are all as described. SURVIVES. Pattern 5 — A4 prose extraction across jurisdictions. None. One federal rule, one JSON Schema file, one CSV dictionary, one validator library. No state layer, no scraper fleet, no PDF mining. SURVIVES cleanly — this is the strongest single feature of the idea. Pattern 6 — dead data with live-looking metadata. Tested by fetching bytes, not metadata: schema file 13,217 bytes HTTP 200; validator npm 2.6.0 published two days ago with four intermediate releases this year; RVU26C zip 6.16 MB with internal member files dated 2026-06-30; Hospital General Information CSV 1.45 MB parsed to 5,419 rows with a sane Hospital Type distribution. Nothing here is a metadata ghost. SURVIVES. Pattern 7 — engine-never-arbiter. The product never decides anything. Every dollar figure is arithmetic the customer could check by hand: gross charge and cash price come straight from their chargemaster; a percentage-of-Medicare term becomes a dollar amount by multiplying their stated percentage against a CMS-published RVU/OPPS value; median and 10th/90th percentiles are order statistics over their own 835 allowed amounts with CMS's own tie rule ('use the next highest observed value'). No model output enters a numeric field. The attestation is signed by the hospital's named CEO or designated senior official — the product populates the block with the name the customer types and never asserts the file is compliant, only that it passed CMS validator version N. Where the customer's 835 extract yields zero rows for a code+payer, the product refuses to emit a percentile and lists that line in a 'cannot compute — no remittance rows in window' report instead of guessing. This is the same shape as run-2's certified-payroll winner: customer's own data, public reference corpus, spec-defined arithmetic, customer signs. SURVIVES.
evidence: Money and pain, all fetched 2026-08-20. (1) Real enforcement dollars: CMS Notice of Imposition of a Civil Monetary Penalty to Pinnacle Hospital, dated June 3 2026, UCN 2026HPT002 — 'A CMP of $51,615.00 was imposed', with the hospital 'remained out of compliance with 45 C.F.R. §§ 180.40 – 180.60' and violations itemised (https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2nd-cmp-notice-pinnacle-redacted.pdf, text extracted locally from the PDF). (2) Scale of exposure right now: 519 hospitals received noncompliance letters between April and early June 2026 across every state but Alaska (Texas 42, California 38, Indiana 34, Louisiana 27) — reported from the list obtained by the AP, June 2026. (3) CMS's own proof that hospitals cannot produce the very field the 2026 rule now doubles down on: in the May 22 2025 HPT guidance implementing EO 14221, CMS reports 'an analysis of a sample of MRF files from large acute care hospitals conducted in February 2025' finding that '63% of the 68 MRFs encode one or more nine 9s for their estimated allowed amount data element values' and '38% of the 68 MRFs sampled encoded nine 9s for more than 90% of their estimated allowed amount data element values'. If large acute-care hospitals with revenue-integrity teams could not derive this number, CAHs cannot — and CY2026 replaces that single field with four harder ones. (4) The hospital lobby concedes the burden: AHA fact sheet dated June 2026 — 'Hospitals dedicate substantial resources to comply with a range of federal and state price transparency requirements' and 'The current approach places a significant administrative burden on hospitals', plus 'CMS has continued to refine these requirements almost annually', which is the recurrence that makes a maintained generator sticky. (5) Capital says the category pays: Turquoise Health announced a $40M Series C led by Oak HC/FT (BusinessWire, March 2026); every provider-facing incumbent I fetched — Turquoise, Rivet, Panacea, PMMC, ClaraPrice — is quote-gated with no published price, the signature of enterprise pricing above what a 25-bed CAH will pay. WHAT I DID NOT PROVE: I could not fetch a single incumbent price or a hospital's contract amount. Willingness-to-pay is inferred from the $51,615 CMP, the 519 letters and the quote-gating, not measured.
pricing_hypothesis: $499 one-time 'Validator Report + Gap List' — upload your currently posted file, get CMS's own validator run against schema v3.0 plus a line-by-line list of what the 2026 rule now requires that your file lacks. This is the wedge a warning letter converts on, and it is a strict artifact, not advice. Then $3,900/yr Single Facility (one CCN, unlimited regenerations, cms-hpt.txt, hosted stable URL, automatic re-generation flag whenever CMS moves the schema), $9,600/yr Multi-Location (up to 4 CCNs, multi-location MRF assembly), $19,000/yr System (up to 10 CCNs, API, dated version ledger export). Annual prepay only — the artifact is annual. Anchored explicitly to the $51,615 CMP and to a fraction of the 0.2–0.4 FTE a CAH currently burns on this, NOT to a competitor price, because no competitor publishes one. That anchor weakness is real and is listed under risks.
moat: Three layers, one of which cannot be backfilled. (1) The generation ledger: every version of every customer's MRF, content-hashed and dated, recorded with the exact schema version and validator version it passed. CMS publishes snapshots of its spec but nothing archives what a given hospital posted on a given day, and hospitals overwrite their own file in place — so when CMS's enforcement letter asks what was public on a date, only a product that has been generating since day one holds the answer. A competitor starting later cannot reconstruct it. (2) The contract-term translation table: mapping 'percentage of a named fee schedule' to a dollar amount requires knowing which fee schedule, which quarterly release, which locality/GPCI and which payment indicator applies — maintained against RVU26A/B/C/D, OPPS addenda, CLFS and DMEPOS each quarter. CMS publishes the files; nobody publishes the mapping, and CMS's May-2025 guidance makes producing that dollar amount mandatory. (3) Structural, not technical: parsing 835s client-side keeps the company outside HIPAA business-associate scope entirely, which is a permanent cost and sales-cycle advantage over any vendor that must sign a BAA, carry cyber cover and pass a security review before a 25-bed hospital can buy.
risks: (1) TOP RISK, NOT DISPROVED: Craneware already gives away Trisus Pricing Transparency free to all US healthcare providers. Its page today says nothing about machine-readable files, v3.0, allowed amounts, percentiles or 2026 — it is a consumer-display and analytics tool scoped to acute-care hospital owners — but Craneware, TruBridge or an EHR could extend a free tier into MRF generation at any time. Nothing in the data or the regulation prevents that; only their focus does. (2) NOT PROVEN: no incumbent price was obtainable — every vendor is quote-gated — so the $3,900/yr hypothesis has no market anchor and could be 3x too high or 3x too low for a CAH. First 20 sales are the experiment. (3) NOT PROVEN: that a CAH CFO will complete a card purchase without procurement. Healthcare buying is slow; the $499 gap report exists partly to test this cheaply. (4) Garbage-in on the 835 extract produces percentile numbers the hospital's CEO then attests to. Mitigation is disclosure, not confidence: the product prints the row count, date range and payer coverage every figure was computed from, refuses to emit any percentile with zero underlying rows, and lists uncomputable lines separately rather than folding them into a headline claim. It must never say 'you are compliant'. (5) Spec churn is both moat and treadmill — CMS revised the validator five times in 2026 alone; a missed schema bump silently degrades every customer's file, which is why staleness detection fails loud and marks files 'regenerate required'. (6) CPT code descriptors are AMA-licensed; the product must consume the customer's own descriptions and CMS-published HCPCS only, and must never redistribute CPT descriptor text. This shapes the UI and must be settled before writing code. (7) Political risk in the other direction: the AHA is lobbying to 'sunset' parts of this framework. A repeal would end the mandate — though the current administration is escalating, not retreating.

name: Outfall
one_liner: Give it your NPDES permit number and your lab's CSV; it returns the month's Discharge Monitoring Report — every summary statistic computed per 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4)(iii) against EPA's own published limit set for your outfalls — as a NetDMR-importable file plus a line-by-line calculation worksheet you can hand an inspector.
artifact: Per monitoring period (monthly for most permittees; quarterly/semiannual/annual for the rest), for each permitted outfall and each parameter: the DMR record set — Value1/Value2/Value3 (e.g. monthly average, daily maximum, daily minimum), the qualifier, unit code, number of excursions, frequency-of-analysis and sample-type codes, and NODI code where no discharge occurred — emitted as (a) a comma-delimited NetDMR import file (.CSV/.TXT/.ZIP, the format NetDMR accepts; Oregon DEQ NetDMR FAQ fetched 2026-08-20 confirms comma-delimited import and points to EPA's import guidance), (b) a print-ready DMR facsimile PDF for the signatory, and (c) a calculation worksheet showing every sample row that fed every reported number and which rule produced it. Submission channel: the customer uploads the file into NetDMR (or their state eDMR) and applies their own 40 CFR 122.22 signature — we never sign, never transmit on their behalf. Cadence: generated on the permit's own monitoring-period schedule, which EPA already publishes per-permit (the ECHO effluent-chart endpoint returns MonitoringPeriodEndDate and DMRDueDate for every limit row — verified live 2026-08-20).
mandate: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4), fetched verbatim from the eCFR versioner API on 2026-08-20 (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-01/title-40.xml?part=122&section=122.41). (l)(4) 'Monitoring reports. Monitoring results shall be reported at the intervals specified elsewhere in this permit.' (i) 'Monitoring results must be reported on a Discharge Monitoring Report (DMR)... As of December 21, 2016 all reports and forms submitted in compliance with this section must be submitted electronically by the permittee to the Director or initial recipient, as defined in 40 CFR 127.2(b)...' (ii) '...the results of such monitoring shall be included in the calculation and reporting of the data submitted in the DMR...' (iii) 'Calculations for all limitations which require averaging of measurements shall utilize an arithmetic mean unless otherwise specified by the Director in the permit.' Two things follow and both are load-bearing: the permittee — not EPA — must perform the calculation, and the regulation names the method. Who must file: every NPDES permittee with monitoring conditions. When: the DMR due date, which EPA itself publishes per limit row (DMRDueDate, e.g. '20-FEB-25' for the January 2025 period on TX0047295, fetched 2026-08-20). Penalty: failure to report is an enforceable permit violation under CWA §309; EPA's compliance coding tracks D80 'Failure to report monitoring data' and D90 'Failure to report data for parameters with effluent limit data', and non-receipt within 31 days of the due date is flagged (Stevens EHS Consulting DMR page, fetched 2026-08-20). ECHO's own CWA query for effective NPDES individual permits returned TotalPenalties of $75,711,186 in the covered window (fetched 2026-08-20).
buyer: The unbundled long tail of NPDES individual permittees. Sourced count: ECHO's CWA REST service, queried 2026-08-20 with p_ptype=NPD&p_pstatus=EFF, returned QueryRows = 92,846 facilities holding effective NPDES individual permits nationally. A single state slice (p_st=IA, same query, same day) returned 1,835. Paging that Iowa result set shows exactly who the long tail is: ADAIR-CASEY COMMUNITY SCHOOL DISTRICT (IA0067156), ADAMS COUNTY CARE FACILITY STP, AFTON CITY PARK SPLASHPAD, ADVANCED HEAT TREAT CORPORATION (IA0075451, IA0078484), A TO Z FEEDERS, ACKLEY CITY OF STP — school districts, care homes, a splash pad, two heat-treat shops, a feedlot, and small-town treatment plants. These are one-operator, no-EHS-department sites. They are self-serve reachable because the entire onboarding is one field: the permit number. Enter IA0067156 and the product pulls that permit's seven parameters, limit values, units, statistical base codes and due dates from a public EPA endpoint in one call, with no configuration and no sales conversation — verified live 2026-08-20. For contrast on how little of this market is served: AllMax, whose Operator10 is the best-known wastewater data package, states it services 'over 2,000 customers around the world' (procurement document fetched 2026-08-20) against 92,846 permits.
input: The customer uploads their commercial lab's electronic data deliverable (CSV/XLSX) plus flow readings — the same file the lab already emails them — and, once, maps its columns. No PHI, no PII: the payload is sample dates, parameter names/codes, concentrations, detection limits and flow volumes for an industrial or municipal outfall. Friction is low because the alternative is already a spreadsheet: Oregon DEQ's NetDMR FAQ (fetched 2026-08-20) answers the question 'I use a spreadsheet now to calculate values based on formulas. Can I upload this data to NetDMR?' — the status quo is hand-built Excel. Nothing about the customer's permit needs to be typed in; that side comes from EPA.

(1) Per-permit limit sets, live JSON: https://echodata.epa.gov/echo/eff_rest_services.get_effluent_chart?p_id={PERMIT}&output=JSON&start_date=..&end_date=.. — fetched 2026-08-20 for TX0047295 (570 KB, HTTP 200) and for Iowa minors IA0067156, IA0075451, IA0078484. (3) The averaging rule itself: eCFR versioner API, 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4)(iii), fetched 2026-08-20 — a versioned XML endpoint, so a rule change is detectable by diff. LIVENESS (kill pattern 6, checked explicitly): the TX0047295 chart for 01/01/2026–08/20/2026 returned 230 rows with monitoring periods running through 30-JUN-26 and ValueReceivedDate values as recent as 20-APR-26, on limit sets that do not expire until 03-JAN-29. This is not metadata-fresh-but-rows-dead; the rows are current-year.
kill_checks: 1 — FREE FIRST-PARTY SUBSTITUTE. EPA's NetDMR is free, and it is the mandated channel — but it validates and transmits, it does not generate. The permitting authority says so in its own words: 'NetDMR is only set up to accept summary statistics, not raw data collected more frequently than monthly. As a result, permittees need to perform calculations on raw data to enter into the eDMR.' (Oregon DEQ NetDMR User's Guide, https://www.oregon.gov/deq/FilterDocs/WQP-guide-NETDMR-Useguide.pdf, PDF downloaded and text-extracted 2026-08-20; the guide then spends pages teaching operators to hand-compute BOD summary statistics.) EPA's Water Pollutant Loading Tool computes pounds from DMRs that have already been submitted — retrospective analytics, not a generator (https://echo.epa.gov/trends/loading-tool/get-data). Verdict: a free validator/transmitter exists; a free generator does not. This is the exemption the brief allows. SURVIVES. 2 — LIVE MICRO-SaaS AT A FRACTION OF THE PRICE. I searched for exactly this and found the opposite: every incumbent is at a multiple, not a fraction. Effluent Labs (https://effluentlabs.com/, fetched 2026-08-20) sells DMR prep and NetDMR submission at $1,500/mo (Essential, 10 parameters), $3,500/mo (Professional), $5,500+/mo (Enterprise) — $18,000–$66,000/yr — and it is a human service ('QA review & flagging', 'dedicated compliance analyst', human 'review & submit'). AllMax Operator10 is desktop, seat-licensed software: a municipal procurement document fetched 2026-08-20 lists 'Operator 10 (Allmax Software) • Total Cost $14,165.00 • Annual Tech Support Cost $1,970.00'. Ecesis DMR Reporting Software (https://www.ecesis.net/Water-Quality-Software/DMR-Reporting-Software.aspx, fetched 2026-08-20) does do the job — 'computes every statistic required for the DMR form' and generates NetDMR files — but publishes no price, offers no self-serve signup ('call (720) 547-5102' or 'SCHEDULE A FREE DEMO'), and sells it as a module of an EHS platform. Klir's DMR press release (klir.com, fetched 2026-08-20) discloses no price and no self-serve path. No indie/self-serve DMR generator surfaced. SURVIVES — the wedge is transparent self-serve pricing, not a cheaper clone. 3 — ALREADY BUNDLED. Partially true, and I will not pretend otherwise: a POTW running Operator10, Hach WIMS or Klir already has this, and an industrial site on an EHS suite has it inside Ecesis. But the bundle's reach is small — AllMax's own procurement sheet claims 'over 2,000 customers around the world' against 92,846 effective individual permits (ECHO, 2026-08-20), and the same sheet records the reviewer rejecting Operator10 as 'very limited in its options', needing a separate LIMS purchase to include the lab. A school district, a splash pad and a heat-treat shop do not buy a $14k desktop plant-data system. SURVIVES for the unbundled tail; fails for large POTWs, so they are not the buyer. 4 — PREMISE VS PRIMARY TEXT. Read the regulation, not a summary: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4)(ii)–(iii) (eCFR API, 2026-08-20) puts the calculation on the permittee and names the method ('arithmetic mean unless otherwise specified by the Director in the permit'). EPA supplies the limit and the statistical base; it does not supply the answer. The premise holds exactly as stated. SURVIVES. 5 — A4/A5 PROSE-EXTRACTION CONFLICT. None. There is no 50-jurisdiction prose corpus and no scraper fleet: the entire per-permit spec arrives as structured JSON from one national EPA endpoint. I verified it works for the hard case — minors, not just majors, where ICIS coverage is historically doubted: IA0067156 (a school district, CWPMajorMinorStatusFlag='N') returned 7 parameters and 283 limit-bearing rows; IA0075451 returned 2 parameters/39 rows; IA0078484 returned 1 parameter/36 rows. All three fetched 2026-08-20. SURVIVES. 6 — DEAD DATA. Checked by pulling rows, not metadata. TX0047295 over 01/01/2026–08/20/2026 returned 230 rows, monitoring periods through 30-JUN-26, newest ValueReceivedDate 20-APR-26; npdes_limits.zip and npdes_dmrs_fy2026.zip are listed as weekly-refresh on ECHO's downloads page (fetched 2026-08-20). SURVIVES. 7 — ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER. The product makes no outcome claim and signs nothing. It does not say 'never miss a deadline'; it does not certify compliance; it does not assert anything about a third party. It performs the arithmetic the CFR prescribes on the customer's own lab numbers against EPA's own published limit row for the customer's own permit, and shows every input on the worksheet. The 40 CFR 122.22 certification stays with the permittee, who uploads and signs in NetDMR. Where a convention is genuinely discretionary (below-detection-limit handling, no-discharge periods), the product does not decide — it exposes the choice as an explicit setting and prints the selected convention on the worksheet. SURVIVES.
evidence: Money is already changing hands for a worse solution, at prices an order of magnitude above the hypothesis. (a) A human service: Effluent Labs charges $1,500/month for monthly DMR prep and NetDMR submission on a single permit with up to 10 parameters, $3,500/month for 25 parameters with a dedicated compliance analyst, and $5,500+/month for multi-permit — i.e. $18k–$66k/yr for work whose deterministic core is a monthly average (https://effluentlabs.com/, fetched 2026-08-20). Its own pitch names the buyer as 'small utilities facing EPA requirements without adequate staffing'. (b) Desktop software: a municipal purchase document lists 'Operator 10 (Allmax Software) • Total Cost $14,165.00 • Annual Tech Support Cost $1,970.00' (https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/cviillega-meet-abc53865e76f4ead838c86705b4ed893/ITEM-Attachment-001-f183742326e64896917d2ae78cf444da.pdf, fetched and text-extracted 2026-08-20). (c) Consultants sell DMR preparation as a service line with no published price (Stevens EHS Consulting, fetched 2026-08-20). (d) The pain, stated by the regulator rather than a vendor: Oregon DEQ's NetDMR User's Guide devotes a section titled 'How do I calculate summary statistics?' to teaching hand calculation because 'NetDMR is only set up to accept summary statistics, not raw data' (fetched 2026-08-20), and its FAQ's answer to 'I use a spreadsheet now to calculate values based on formulas' documents that the incumbent tool is Excel.
pricing_hypothesis: $89/month per permit for a single outfall with up to 12 parameters; $199/month for multi-outfall permits; $499/month for a portfolio of up to 10 permits (contract operators, consultants, multi-site industrials). Annual prepay at ten months. The anchor is explicit and public: the cheapest human alternative found is $1,500/month for one permit and ten parameters, and the cheapest software alternative found is a $14,165 desktop licence plus $1,970/yr support. A $89/month self-serve price is 6% of the human service and pays back the desktop licence in year one, while sitting under the threshold at which a school district or a heat-treat shop needs a purchase order.
moat: Four layers, in order of durability. (1) The onboarding is the moat's front door: permit number in, complete limit set out, in one public API call — no configuration, no discovery call, no implementation project. Every incumbent found requires a demo, a quote, or an install; that gap is structural, not a feature. (2) A compounding library of lab EDD column mappings. Commercial labs emit dozens of deliverable layouts; each new lab format learned makes the next customer of that lab zero-touch, and the mapping library is private data that no public corpus contains. (3) The calculation ledger. Every reported value stays linked to the sample rows that produced it and the CFR clause that governed it, retained across years. That ledger is what a permittee hands an inspector and what makes a DMR defensible; it is also what makes leaving expensive, because it does not export into anyone else's model. (4) Adjacency on the same corpus and the same buyer, with no new customer acquisition: the biosolids annual program report under 40 CFR 503.18 (pollutant concentrations against the 503.13 tables, annual whole-sludge application rate, cumulative pollutant loading rate) and NPDES pretreatment periodic reports run on identical inputs — customer lab data plus a CFR table — and can be added as modules rather than as a second company.
risks: Format fragmentation across states is the real one: NetDMR is EPA's tool, but states may 'develop their own tools' (EPA NPDES eReporting page, fetched 2026-08-20, last updated 2026-02-12), and California, Ohio, North Carolina and Pennsylvania run their own eDMR systems with their own import formats. I could not obtain a definitive NetDMR-vs-state-eDMR state list today; EPA's page declines to enumerate it. Mitigation is to ship NetDMR-format only and gate signup on the permit's state, but the addressable share of the 92,846 permits is therefore NOT YET PROVEN. Second: a residual prose dependency. Below-detection-limit averaging conventions and no-discharge (NODI) handling are sometimes specified in the permit document rather than in ICIS, so a thin slice of the spec still lives in a PDF the product does not read; the product must surface these as customer-set, worksheet-printed choices rather than silently deciding — and that is a product-design constraint, not a solved problem. Third: lab deliverables. Determinism holds only if intake is constrained to CSV/XLSX and a fixed set of EDD layouts; the moment scanned PDF lab reports are accepted, extraction judgment enters and the A4 gate is at risk. Fourth: ICIS limit-set lag after a permit is reissued — the new limits may not appear promptly, and generating against a stale limit row is the failure mode that would hurt most. Fifth: bundling, honestly — POTWs on Operator10, WIMS or Klir are not winnable and should not be marketed to. NOT YET PROVEN, beyond the state-coverage question: (i) what fraction of the 92,846 effective individual permits carry monthly rather than annual or no monitoring obligations; (ii) whether a NetDMR import file generated end-to-end is actually accepted by NetDMR's edit checks — I read the format's existence and the agency's guidance but have never submitted one; (iii) willingness of a sub-$200/month municipal or small-industrial buyer to pay by card without a procurement process; (iv) whether ICIS statistical base codes alone are sufficient to reproduce every DMR value type, or whether some parameters need permit-specific rules.

name: CallFile
one_liner: Turns a money services business's own transaction ledger export into the complete NMLS MSB Call Report XML — financial condition, company-wide activity, one state component per licensed state, permissible investments, and Q4 destination-country detail — schema-valid against NMLS's published XSD and ready for the licensee to upload and submit themselves.
artifact: One XML file per reporting quarter conforming to the NMLS-published MSBCR schema for the licensee's current Form Version (today FV4: schema file `ExternalMsbcrBatchFileSchemaV4.txt`, field spec `MSBCR Data Specification v4.xlsx`, sample `EXTERNAL_MSBCR_2024_Q4.xml`, all listed live on NMLS's MSBCR XML Specification page fetched 2026-08-20). The file contains the components the spec defines: FC (Financial Condition), TA (company-wide Transaction Activity), one ST component per state the licensee is licensed in, PI (Permissible Investments), and TD-A/TD-B (Transaction Destination Country) which per MTMA s.7.01(c) is only carried in the Q4 report. Shipped alongside it: a reconciliation PDF that shows, for every single figure in the XML, the arithmetic and the exact uploaded ledger rows it came from, so the officer who signs can audit it before submitting. Cadence: quarterly, keyed to the 45-days-after-quarter-end deadline (Q1 due ~May 15, Q2 ~Aug 14, Q3 ~Nov 14, Q4 ~Feb 14). Channel: the customer downloads the XML and uploads it in NMLS themselves — the spec is explicit that 'the upload process will not submit your MSBCR filing. You must manually run completeness checks against each component and submit the filing in NMLS' (MSB Call Report XML Specification, Release 2024.8, rev 10/2/2024, fetched and text-extracted 2026-08-20). We generate; NMLS validates; the licensee signs and files. We never touch NMLS.
mandate: CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act s.7.01 'Report of Condition' — fetched and text-extracted from https://www.csbs.org/sites/default/files/2023-02/CSBS%20Money%20Transmission%20Modernization%20Act.pdf on 2026-08-20: '(a) Each licensee shall submit a report of condition within 45 days of the end of the calendar quarter... (b) The report of condition shall include: (1) Financial information at the licensee level; (2) Nationwide and state-specific money transmission transaction information in every jurisdiction in the United States where the licensee is licensed to engage in money transmission; (3) Permissible investments report; (4) Transaction destination country reporting for money received for transmission, if applicable.' Footnote 19 of the model act states plainly: 'This language is designed to implement state use of the NMLS MSB Call Report.' Enacted-state confirmation, fetched 2026-08-20: Georgia DBF, https://dbf.georgia.gov/money-service-businesses/quarterly-msb-reporting — 'Companies must file a quarterly MSB Call Report through the NMLS'; 'Required quarterly reporting must be completed within 45 days after the quarter end'; 'Licensees that fail to file required reports by the deadline will be assessed a fine of $1,000 per report not filed timely and may subject their Georgia license to revocation.' Scope of the mandate, from NMLS's own 2023 MSB Annual Report (fetched + extracted 2026-08-20): 'In 2023, 36 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico required their licensed companies to file the MSB Call Report, an increase of two states during the year.' Still expanding in 2026: FS Vector (pub. 2026-06-17, fetched 2026-08-20) reports Illinois now requires both Financial Condition and state-specific transaction MSB Call Reports quarterly within 45 days starting Q1 2026, and North Dakota newly requires the State Transactions Destination Country Detail Section.
buyer: State-licensed money services businesses that file the MSB Call Report — money transmitters, stored-value/prepaid issuers, virtual-currency exchangers, check cashers, currency exchangers. Sourced counts, all from NMLS's own 2023 MSB Annual Report (fetched + text-extracted 2026-08-20): 2,804 MSB companies in NMLS holding 10,960 approved licenses; 555 companies reported activity on the MSB Call Report nationwide totals; 611 companies licensed as money transmitters holding 8,589 money transmitter licenses, of which 343 reported money transmission on the call report. The pain scales with state count, and NMLS publishes that too: 'the average money transmitter conducted business in 14 states, and the average stored value company conducted business in 30 states', virtual currency exchanging companies average 27 states. So the median buyer assembles 14-30 separate ST components every 90 days. Self-serve reachable because these are venture-funded or owner-operated fintechs with an in-house compliance officer and a card, not procurement committees — and because the alternative they price against is consulting: InnReg (updated 2025-12-11, fetched 2026-08-20) puts money-transmitter consulting firms at '$5,000 to $20,000 per state' and compliance software at '$10,000 to $100,000 per year', so a four-figure annual tool is below the noise floor of their existing spend.
input: The licensee's own transaction ledger export plus a small balance-sheet mapping. Concretely: (a) a transaction-level CSV from their core ledger / PSP / banking partner with date, amount, product type (transmission, payment instrument, stored value, check cashing, currency exchange, virtual currency), sender state, recipient state, recipient country; (b) daily outstanding-transmission-liability snapshots (needed because the NMLS FAQ, fetched 2026-08-20, defines it as 'the average sum of the daily amounts of a licensee's total outstanding money transmissions' over the quarter); (c) a one-time chart-of-accounts mapping from their trial balance to the FC and PI line items, stored and reused every quarter. Friction is one CSV export plus a first-quarter mapping session done in-product. NO PII TRAP BY DESIGN: none of the MSBCR components require a customer name, address, account number or SSN — the report is counts, dollar aggregates, states and ISO country codes. The parser therefore accepts only the columns it needs and drops/refuses identity columns at ingest, which keeps the product out of GLBA-customer-data scope and out of any breach-notification exposure. That is a deliberate design constraint, not an afterthought.

(1) NMLS MSB Call Report XML Specification page — https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/msbCR/licensing/msbCR/topics/msbCR_XMLspecs.html — fetched today, lists per-Form-Version downloadable artifacts: FV4 `ExternalMsbcrBatchFileSchemaV4.txt` (the XSD), `MSBCR Data Specification v4.xlsx` (the field spec as a spreadsheet — directly parseable), `EXTERNAL_MSBCR_2024_Q4.xml` (sample), plus the equivalents for FV3 and FV2. kill_checks: PATTERN 1 — free first-party generator. NMLS publishes the spec but ships no generator. Fetched today, https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/knowledge/Products/nmls/pubs/msbCR/licensing/msbCR/topics/msbCR_overviewDefinitions.html: NMLS offers 'NMLS MSB Call Report Sections and Definitions' (field definitions) and upload specifications — 'The MSB Call Report can be uploaded as a comma-separated values (CSV) or eXtensible Markup Language (XML) file' — and no downloadable template, workbook or computational tool; licensees are responsible for compiling their own data to the published field spec. What NMLS DOES ship free is a VALIDATOR: the spec PDF (fetched) documents Level 1 (immediate, schema) and Level 2 (queued, business-rule) validations on upload. Per the brief, a free validator that does not generate is the acceptable case, and it is actively good for us — the government system, not our model, is the arbiter of whether a file is correct. Contrast with the two ideas this killed elsewhere: CFPB ships an actual free GENERATOR for HMDA ('The data is now formatted into a pipe delimited text file... ready to be submitted to the HMDA Platform', https://ffiec.cfpb.gov/documentation/tools/lar-formatting/, fetched today) and the FEC ships free filing software ('FECfile+, the new web-based version of FECFile, is the free electronic filing software for committees', https://www.fec.gov/help-candidates-and-committees/filing-reports/electronic-filing/getting-started-fecfile-plus/, fetched today). Neither analogue exists here. PATTERN 2 — live micro-SaaS incumbent. Six distinct searches run today ('MSB Call Report software vendor automate preparation pricing', 'MSB Call Report automate generate NMLS filing tool startup SaaS', 'MSBCR XML generator tool money transmitter software', 'MSB call report preparation service fee per quarter', 'call report preparation money transmitter consultant fee', 'Upwork/freelancer MSB call report'). Zero products surfaced that generate the MSBCR. Every hit was either NMLS's own documentation, a state regulator page, or an AML/KYC vendor. The nearest adjacent commercial actor is ComplyOne (https://complyone.tech/blog/money-transmitter-license-annual-reporting-requirements, fetched today) which sells 'Compliance, however you need it: software, advisory, or both' to 'manage their multi-state annual reporting calendar, prepare and submit annual filings' — annual filings and calendar management, no MSBCR generation claim, and no published price (quote-gated, i.e. the incumbent motion is human advisory, exactly the shape the factory's two prior winners displaced). PATTERN 3 — bundled in software the buyer already pays for. Checked the category leader in MSB regulatory reporting: Alessa's MSB regulatory-reporting page (https://alessa.com/software-solutions/aml-compliance/regulatory-reporting/msbs/, fetched today) enumerates every report it produces — FinCEN CTR, SAR, Form 8300; FINTRAC LCTR/STR/CDR/LVCTR/EFT; plus Jamaica, Dominican Republic, Cambodia, Cyprus, Mexico, Philippines filings — and the NMLS MSB Call Report appears nowhere. That is a structural, not accidental, gap: AML platforms exist to detect and report suspicion transaction-by-transaction; the MSBCR is a state-by-state financial and volume aggregation, a different data plane. This is precisely the check that killed the NMLS MORTGAGE Call Report, where the same job IS bundled: LendingPad's own knowledge base (https://kb.lendingpad.com/how-to-file-nmls-call-report-mcr, fetched today) walks brokers through generating the MCR and exporting it as XML inside the LOS they already pay for. MSBs have no equivalent dominant operational system. PATTERN 4 — premise vs primary text. Verified against the model statute itself, not commentary: MTMA s.7.01 quoted verbatim above, 45 days, five enumerated contents, footnote 19 tying it to the NMLS MSB Call Report; s.7.01(c) restricting destination-country data to the Q4 report; and s.7.03 imposing a SECOND quarterly artifact (the authorized-delegate report, 12 enumerated fields). The agency does not compute anything — the NMLS FAQ (fetched today) is explicit that the licensee computes and must be able to defend its own figures: 'Virtual currency valuation must be in U.S. Dollars and should be based on a generally accepted exchange rate and the licensee, when requested, should be able to document and substantiate how they arrived at the valuation', and average daily outstanding transmission liability is defined as a metric the licensee derives. PATTERN 5 — A4 / 50-jurisdiction prose. Does not apply. There is ONE national form with ONE versioned XSD; state variation is expressed as repeated ST components inside that single schema, keyed by state code, not as fifty bodies of prose to extract. And the per-state 'which components do I owe' question is answered by NMLS itself, not by us: the spec (fetched) states NMLS 'will create any missing, but required components automatically when creating an MSBCR filing for a quarterly period type'. We generate for every state the licensee is licensed in and let NMLS's own configuration arbitrate. PATTERN 6 — dead data. The corpus is a versioned spec plus a live change stream, and both were checked today. Change log in the fetched spec runs to 2024-10-02 / Release 2024.8; the spec page lists three concurrent Form Versions (FV2, FV3, FV4) with their own schemas; and the form is demonstrably moving in 2026 — NMLS public comment on MSBCR updates closed 2026-07-20, Illinois changed its requirement for Q1 2026, North Dakota added the TD section, Florida revised its parallel state form effective 2026-07-01 (all FS Vector, pub. 2026-06-17 and 2026-06-18, both fetched today). No live-looking-but-frozen metadata: a new Form Version announces itself as a new XSD filename on a page we diff weekly. PATTERN 7 — engine-never-arbiter. The product never asserts a number of its own invention and never files. Every figure in the XML is a deterministic aggregation of rows the customer uploaded, and the reconciliation PDF shows the arithmetic and the source rows for each one. The two genuinely judgmental inputs are declared and pushed to the customer: which balance-sheet lines are permissible investments, and which exchange rate substantiates virtual currency valuation — both are asked once, stored as the customer's own stated policy, and reprinted verbatim in the reconciliation so the signer owns them. Correctness of the file is adjudicated by NMLS's Level 1/Level 2 validators, not by us. Submission is adjudicated by the licensee: the spec's own words, 'the upload process will not submit your MSBCR filing. You must manually run completeness checks against each component and submit the filing in NMLS.' We make no 'never miss a deadline' or 'compliant' claim — we produce a file and show our work.

(3) ComplyOne sells multi-state licensee reporting as 'software, advisory, or both' with prices withheld behind a quote (https://complyone.tech/blog/money-transmitter-license-annual-reporting-requirements) — quote-gated advisory is the tell that the work is currently done by people. (4) The cost of NOT doing it is published by the regulator: Georgia DBF (https://dbf.georgia.gov/money-service-businesses/quarterly-msb-reporting) — '$1,000 per report not filed timely and may subject their Georgia license to revocation'; a licensee in 14 states faces that exposure fourteen times a quarter. (5) Volume proving the work exists at scale: NMLS's 2023 MSB Annual Report records $5.85 trillion in reported MSB activity across 555 reporting companies, with the average money transmitter operating in 14 states and the average stored-value company in 30. NOT YET PROVEN, stated plainly: I could not fetch a single published per-filing or per-quarter price for MSB Call Report preparation. Every consulting price above is for the surrounding category, not the artifact. That is the softest joint in this idea and the first thing to test with real buyers.
pricing_hypothesis: Per-quarter, priced on licensed-state count because that is what the work scales with. Solo $249/quarter (up to 3 licensed states, FC + TA + ST + PI, schema-validated XML plus reconciliation PDF). Multi-state $749/quarter (up to 20 states, Q4 destination-country TD-A/TD-B, amendment regeneration against a processed filing, prior-quarter variance report). Fleet $1,749/quarter (unlimited states, the s.7.03 authorized-delegate quarterly file, Form-Version migration when NMLS ships a new schema, API ingest). Annual prepay -20%. Anchored against '$5,000 to $20,000 per state' consulting and '$10,000 to $100,000 per year' compliance software (InnReg, fetched 2026-08-20): the Multi-state tier is ~$3,000/year, i.e. less than the consulting fee for a single state, which makes the comparison arithmetic rather than rhetorical. Natural expansion axis is state count, which grows every time the licensee adds a license — revenue compounds with the customer's own licensing roadmap with zero sales motion.
moat: Three layers, none of them the spec itself (which is public). (1) The ingest mapping library: a growing set of validated transformations from real-world source shapes — core-ledger exports, PSP settlement files, banking-partner statements, blockchain custody reports — into MSBCR field semantics. Each customer's first quarter contributes a mapping; the hundredth customer onboards in minutes. (2) The Form-Version migration engine. NMLS runs multiple concurrent Form Versions (FV2, FV3, FV4 all published today) and a new one is in flight after the comment period that closed 2026-07-20. Every version break is a moment when the customer's homegrown spreadsheet silently produces an invalid file and ours does not. Maintaining correct mappings across versions is unglamorous, continuous, and exactly what a consultant charges for. (3) The customer's own filing archive. We keep every generated quarter, so from quarter two onward the product does something no fresh entrant can: quarter-over-quarter variance checking on each state's figures before the file is emitted, and one-click regeneration of an amendment (the spec's merge rules, fetched today, define exactly how an amendment overlays a processed filing, and NMLS permits amendment for 24 months after the filing period). None of these is patentable; all of them take quarters of accumulation.
risks: (1) SMALL TAM, the biggest risk and it is sourced, not guessed: NMLS's own 2023 report counts 2,804 MSB companies in NMLS and only 555 reporting on the call report's nationwide totals. Realistic serviceable pool is roughly 600-1,200 filers. At the Multi-state tier a 10% share is ~$180-350k ARR — a real autonomous company, but not a large one, and it caps the upside hard. (2) NOT PROVEN: no fetched per-filing price for MSBCR preparation anywhere. The willingness-to-pay number is inferred from adjacent consulting rates and must be tested first. (3) INPUT AVAILABILITY: average daily outstanding transmission liability requires daily liability snapshots across the quarter. Some licensees do not retain them. Where they are missing the product must refuse to compute the metric and say so, not interpolate — which may block generation for a subset of buyers entirely. (4) PARALLEL STATE FORMS: the MSBCR is not universal. Florida runs its own Form OFR-560-04, revised effective 2026-07-01 (FS Vector, fetched today), and California DFPI publishes its own money transmitter call report forms (surfaced in search today at dfpi.ca.gov, NOT fetched — must be verified before any coverage claim). So 'one file covers everything' is false for at least two large states, and the honest v1 promise is the NMLS MSBCR only. (5) SPEC CHURN IN FLIGHT: the NMLS comment period on MSBCR updates closed 2026-07-20; a new Form Version could land mid-build. This is the moat and the hazard at once. (6) NMLS/CSBS could ship a free converter, as CFPB did for HMDA — that single event would end this business, and there is no defence except being the incumbent when it happens. (7) ComplyOne or FS Vector could productise the same generator; their advantage is customer relationships, ours is that they sell hours. (8) Permissible-investment categorisation is genuinely legal in nature; the product must present it as the customer's stated policy every quarter, never as our determination, or it drifts into arbiter territory.

name: LaborRoll
one_liner: Generates the California CRD Labor Contractor Employee Report — the one mandatory pay-data filing that payroll systems structurally cannot produce, because the worker-level data lives inside the staffing agencies, not the client employer's payroll.
artifact: Two deterministic files, both to CRD's published reporting-year spec. (1) LABOR CONTRACTOR EXTRACT — one file per client employer, generated from the staffing agency's own payroll/timekeeping export, carrying the worker-level rows CRD requires: establishment, job category, race/ethnicity, sex, exempt/nonexempt status, employment type (full-time / part-time / intermittent), pay band derived from W-2 Box 5 earnings, hours worked, total annual weeks worked, labor contractor FEIN. (2) LABOR CONTRACTOR EMPLOYEE REPORT — the consolidated master file in CRD's Excel template or CRD's published CSV layout that the client employer uploads to the CRD Pay Data Portal, with computed employee counts and the MEDIAN and MEAN hourly rate for every establishment x job category x race/ethnicity x sex x pay band cell. Cadence: annual, on a snapshot payroll period the filer selects between Oct 1 and Dec 31, submitted on or before the second Wednesday of May (May 12, 2027 for reporting year 2026). Channel: the customer uploads to CRD's portal and certifies — the product never files and never signs.
mandate: California Government Code section 12999, as enacted/amended by SB 1162, fetched today from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (the official California legislative site) via the SB 1162 bill text. Verbatim from that text: 'a private employer that has 100 or more employees hired through labor contractors within the prior calendar year shall submit a separate pay data report to the department'; 'Within each job category, for each combination of race, ethnicity, and sex, the median and mean hourly rate'; 'On or before the second Wednesday of May 2023, and on or before the second Wednesday of May of each year thereafter'. Subdivision (f) sets civil penalties of up to $100 per employee for an initial failure to file and up to $200 per employee for subsequent failures, payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund. WHO MUST FILE: a private client employer with 100 or more labor contractor employees (nationwide) and at least one in California. WHEN: annually, second Wednesday of May. CRD's own page (fetched 2026-08-20) confirms the requirement and the May 13, 2026 date for reporting year 2025; Jackson Lewis (fetched 2026-08-20) confirms mandatory penalties are now enforced for the 2026 cycle.
buyer: PRIMARY: California labor contractors — staffing, ag-labor, janitorial, warehouse/light-industrial and hospitality-supply firms — each of which receives a separate, differently-formatted data request from every client employer it places workers with, every spring. They already hold the data in their own payroll and timekeeping systems, so the job is file-in / file-out with no integration. SECONDARY: client employers with 100+ labor contractor employees, who must consolidate every contractor's file into one master submission and are the party CRD penalizes. Self-serve reachable because there is nothing to connect: the entire transaction is upload an export, download a CRD-format file. HONEST GAP: I could NOT source a filer count today. CRD has published no reporting-year-2025 filing statistics (searched 2026-08-20, nothing returned), so the size of the labor-contractor filer population is UNPROVEN and must be sized before build.
input: One payroll/timekeeping export (CSV or XLSX) from the labor contractor, or the set of contractor extracts for a client employer. Every required column already exists in payroll: client employer, worksite address, job title, race/ethnicity, sex, exempt/nonexempt, full-time/part-time/intermittent, W-2 Box 5 earnings, hours worked, weeks worked. Friction is one upload. NO PHI/PII TRAP BY DESIGN: CRD's report is aggregated, so no names, SSNs or dates of birth are required — the parser rejects identifier columns outright and refuses the file if they are present, keeping the product out of identifiable-worker data entirely.
corpus: (1) CRD's published reporting-year templates, CSV submission examples, User Guide and Handbook — calcivilrights.ca.gov/paydatareporting/ fetched 2026-08-20, which lists an Excel template, CSV submission examples, a portal user guide and a handbook; CRD reissued the official reporting-year-2025 files in January 2026, so cadence is annual (January) reissue. (2) Census NAICS 2022 code list — https://www.census.gov/naics/2022NAICS/2-6%20digit_2022_Codes.xlsx — fetched 2026-08-20, HTTP 200, content-type application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet; revised on a 5-year cycle (2022 current, 2027 next). (3) O*NET / SOC 2018 occupational taxonomy — https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html fetched 2026-08-20, current release O*NET 30.3, published simultaneously in Excel, CSV, JSON, MySQL, JSON-LD, RDF/XML and Turtle; the database file endpoint https://www.onetcenter.org/dl_files/database/db_29_2_text.zip returned HTTP 200 today. Point releases ship quarterly. This corpus becomes load-bearing for reporting year 2026, when CRD replaces the 10 EEO-1 job categories with 23 SOC-aligned categories (CDF Labor Law, fetched 2026-08-20). STALENESS DETECTION: hash CRD's template files; if the reporting-year template has not been reissued by February 1, the product fails closed, suppresses report generation and shows the last verified template date rather than emitting a file against a stale spec.
kill_checks: 1) FREE FIRST-PARTY SUBSTITUTE — SURVIVES on the stated exception. CRD ships a free portal, blank Excel templates, CSV examples, a user guide and a handbook (calcivilrights.ca.gov/paydatareporting/, fetched 2026-08-20). The portal VALIDATES on upload; it does not GENERATE. There is no CRD tool that turns a payroll export into a report, and no CRD mechanism at all for collecting data from labor contractors — CRD's own instructed method is to email each labor contractor, have it pick its own snapshot period, then hand-consolidate every file into one master (CRD guidance surfaced 2026-08-20). 2) LIVE MICRO-SAAS INCUMBENTS — searched twice today. The only self-serve-looking site, californiapaydatareporting.com (fetched 2026-08-20), publishes NO pricing, offers 'Start For Free' and routes to 'an expert' — a consultant funnel, not a generator. Affirmity and Syndio sell state pay-data software but quote-only/enterprise; OutSolve, Berkshire and Trusaic are human consultancies. No cheap self-serve generator for the Labor Contractor report was found. 3) BUNDLING — the decisive check, and it passes STRUCTURALLY, not just today. Greenshades' own post (fetched 2026-08-20) states it generates 'a California Payroll Employee Report, generated directly from your payroll system as a downloadable .xlsx file', and then says only that 'the Labor Contractor Employee Report covers workers supplied through a third-party labor contractor' and 'carries separate requirements and its own filing complexities' — it does not produce it. It cannot: the worker-level rows sit in the labor contractor's payroll, not the client's. This is why I killed the Payroll Employee Report as a standalone (bundled in Greenshades and Dayforce) and kept only the half payroll cannot reach. 4) PREMISE VS PRIMARY TEXT — verified against Gov Code 12999 itself (leginfo, fetched 2026-08-20), not against commentary. CRD does not compute the medians or means; the filer must. 5) A4 — one jurisdiction, one published spec, one portal. No prose extraction across states, no scraper fleet. 6) DEAD DATA — corpus endpoints fetched today: NAICS XLSX HTTP 200, O*NET 30.3 HTTP 200 with a current versioned release; CRD reissued official RY2025 files in January 2026. The live-looking-but-dead risk is CRD's template page, handled by the hash-and-fail-closed rule above. 7) ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER — every number is arithmetic over the customer's own rows: counts, pay-band assignment from W-2 Box 5 earnings, mean and median hourly rate. No model produces a rate, a classification or a decision. The product never files and never certifies; the client employer uploads and signs. Rows that cannot be assigned a job category or establishment go into a visible 'unassigned' bucket, are excluded from every computed cell, and the emitted file carries a dated caveat naming the excluded count.
evidence: (a) The work is being done by hand today, at the employer's cost: CDF Labor Law's analysis (https://www.cdflaborlaw.com/blog/changes-to-2025-crd-pay-data-reporting-new-fields-new-complexity, fetched 2026-08-20) documents three NEW mandatory fields for reporting year 2025 on both reports — exemption status, employment type (full-time/part-time/intermittent), and total annual weeks worked — and states plainly that 'Data often resides across separate HR, timekeeping, and payroll systems, demanding coordinated extraction and aggregation.' It also confirms the reporting-year-2026 move from 10 EEO-1 categories to 23 SOC-aligned categories. (b) CRD's own prescribed process is email-and-spreadsheet consolidation across contractors (CRD guidance surfaced 2026-08-20). (c) Human consultancies sell exactly this: OutSolve (https://www.outsolve.com/what-is-california-pay-data-reporting), Berkshire and Trusaic all market California pay data reporting services, all quote-gated; OutSolve alone completes over 17,000 compliance plans a year for more than 1,700 organizations (outsolve.com, surfaced 2026-08-20) — a consultant business at scale, which is the incumbent shape the winning pattern predicts. (d) A dedicated expert-funnel domain exists purely for this filing (californiapaydatareporting.com, fetched 2026-08-20). (e) Statutory downside anchoring willingness to pay: $100 per employee, then $200 per employee (Gov Code 12999(f), fetched today). HONEST GAP: I did not obtain a published per-report consultant price today — every incumbent is quote-gated. That quote wall is the pattern-2 opening, but it is NOT proof of a price point, and a real number must be obtained before pricing is set.
pricing_hypothesis: Supply side (labor contractors): $299 per client-employer extract, or $1,499/year flat for unlimited extracts — a staffing firm placing workers with 20 client employers currently rebuilds 20 differently-shaped spreadsheets each spring. Demand side (client employers): $999 for the consolidated, portal-ready Labor Contractor Employee Report; $2,499 for the bundle that also emits the Payroll Employee Report for employers not on Greenshades/Dayforce/ADP. Anchored against a $100-$200 per-employee statutory penalty (a 300-worker exposure is $30,000-$60,000) and against quote-gated consultants, not against a known incumbent price.
moat: Thin technically, real operationally, and it compounds. (a) The reporting-year-2026 replacement of 10 EEO-1 categories with 23 SOC-aligned categories invalidates every mapping every filer has — a maintained job-title-to-SOC crosswalk built on O*NET, plus each customer's own ratified crosswalk, is an asset that is painful to rebuild elsewhere and is re-ratified rather than re-created each year. (b) The labor contractor sits on the supply side of a many-to-many file exchange: once its client employers are receiving our extract format, switching cost lands on the client side too, which is the wrong side for a competitor to attack. (c) Archiving each customer's snapshot files makes year two a diff rather than a rebuild, and no same-day entrant can backfill last year's snapshot. (d) The structural bundling gap in (3) is not a roadmap item a payroll vendor can close — it would have to reach into a third party's payroll.
risks: 1) SEASONALITY IS THE BIGGEST WEAKNESS AND IT IS NOT SMALL: the CRD portal opens around February and the deadline is the second Wednesday of May. Work does start earlier — the snapshot period must be chosen and frozen between Oct 1 and Dec 31, so the supply-side product has a real Q4 2026 entry point — but first revenue is realistically November 2026 to February 2027, not weeks from launch. A factory optimising for time-to-first-revenue should treat this as a strike. 2) NOT PROVEN: the number of labor-contractor filers. CRD has published no RY2025 filing statistics; the buyer population is unsized. 3) NOT PROVEN: any published consultant price. Every incumbent is quote-gated, so the price umbrella is inferred, not measured. 4) Single jurisdiction. CRD could add a labor-contractor collection or generation feature to its portal and collapse the wedge in one release — this is the single most likely killer and should be watched in CRD's January template drop. 5) CRD has not yet published the reporting-year-2026 (23-category SOC) template; building the crosswalk ahead of the published spec is speculative and must fail closed until the template lands. 6) A payroll vendor could bolt on a labor-contractor import path; the defence is entering from the staffing-agency side, which payroll vendors do not serve. 7) Even de-identified, worker-level pay-plus-race rows are sensitive; the identifier-rejecting parser is a hard requirement, not a nicety. 8) The whole angle assigned to me was otherwise a graveyard (see rejected list) — this idea survives on a narrow structural gap, and if that gap closes there is no fallback within the angle.

name: Basic Model
one_liner: Upload your models and their lab test values once; get back the DOE-format annual certification report file for every basic model you sell, plus the print-ready FTC EnergyGuide label artwork with the 16 CFR 305 arithmetic already done — regenerated automatically every year and every time the CFR tables move.
artifact: Two artifacts from one dataset, both mandatory and both recurring. (1) The DOE annual certification report: one row per basic model in DOE's product-specific Excel certification template (the exact template version DOE currently publishes for that product/equipment class), packaged with the compliance statement fields required by 10 CFR 429.12(b)-(c), ready for the customer to upload to CCMS under their own registered account. Cadence: 'before distributing in commerce ... and annually thereafter' (10 CFR 429.12(a)), which for the 16 CFR 305 labeled categories has hard published per-category dates — Portable air conditioners Feb 1; fluorescent lamp ballasts, showerheads and faucets Mar 1; water heaters, furnaces and pool heaters May 1; dishwashers Jun 1; central AC, heat pumps and room ACs Jul 1; refrigerators/refrigerator-freezers/freezers Aug 1; clothes washers Oct 1 (16 CFR 305.11(b)(1) Table 1, fetched today). So the product has a filing event nearly every month of the year, not one annual spike. (2) The EnergyGuide label: a print-ready vector label (and the web-resolution image required by 16 CFR 305.9 and the label URL required by 16 CFR 305.11(a)(5)) with the Estimated Yearly Energy Cost computed from the customer's own certified test value times the Representative Average Unit Energy Cost in Appendix K1/K2 to Part 305, the marker positioned on the comparability range taken from the correct product-class appendix (A1-J2), the prescribed rounding, and — where the model falls outside the current published range — the exact substitute sentence 16 CFR 305.12(c) requires instead of a marker. Delivery: web app plus emailed dated bundle (xlsx + PDF/SVG + a citation sheet showing every number's CFR source).
mandate: Primary text fetched from the eCFR API today (2026-08-20), not from memory. 10 CFR 429.12(a): 'Each manufacturer, before distributing in commerce any basic model of a covered product or covered equipment subject to an applicable energy conservation standard set forth in parts 430 or 431, and annually thereafter on or before the dates provided in paragraph (d) of this section, shall submit a certification report to DOE certifying that each basic model meets the applicable energy conservation standard(s).' 429.12(b) enumerates the required fields; 429.12(c) requires a signed compliance statement naming a company official. 16 CFR 305.11(a)(1): 'each manufacturer of a covered product ... shall submit annually a report for each model in current production containing the same information that must be submitted to the Department of Energy pursuant to 10 CFR part 429', satisfiable via CCMS. 16 CFR 305.11(a)(5) additionally requires submitting a URL for each online EnergyGuide label. Who must file: manufacturers AND importers — DOE's own database banner states 'Each importer must submit a valid certification report for each model it imports, even if the model already appears on this web site' (fetched today). Hard forward trigger, quoted verbatim from 16 CFR 305.12(a) fetched today: 'The Commission shall publish revised ranges in the Federal Register in 2027. When the ranges are revised, all information disseminated after 90 days following the publication of the revision shall conform to the revised ranges.' 305.12(b) says the same for the Representative Average Unit Energy Cost figures. That is a dated, published, industry-wide forced regeneration of every label in 2027 — the single largest artifact-generation event in this space, and it is in the regulation today. Penalty: EPCA civil penalties per unit under 42 U.S.C. 6303/6316 plus retail delisting; DOE's certification program is the enforcement gate for distribution in commerce.
buyer: DOE's own Paperwork Reduction Act notice for this exact collection (89 FR 80235-36, published 2024-10-02, full text fetched today) states: 'Annual Estimated Number of Respondents: 2,083; Annual Estimated Number of Total Responses: 32,243; Annual Estimated Number of Burden Hours: 775,965 (35 hours per certification ...)' and 'Annual Estimated Reporting and Recordkeeping Cost Burden: $56,645,445.00'. That is 2,083 named, countable, obligated companies carrying ~$27,193 each per year of certification paperwork cost by the regulator's own arithmetic, across DOE's 65+ covered product and equipment categories (consumer appliances plus external power supplies, battery chargers, air cleaners, portable ACs, dedicated-purpose pool pump motors, commercial pumps, compressors, walk-in coolers, commercial water heating). The segment that is self-serve reachable is the importer tail: brands and importers of LED lamps, power supplies, battery chargers, ceiling fans, air cleaners, portable ACs and dehumidifiers, who have no in-house regulatory engineer, no Illustrator seat, and who get hit first by retail enforcement (Amazon blocks ASINs for missing EnergyGuide label images — multiple Seller Central forum threads on 'Energy Guide Label Requirement' and 'Incorrectly Restricted' surfaced in search today, though Seller Central requires login and was NOT fetched, so this is flagged unproven). The third-party representative channel is the second buyer: DOE explicitly permits 'importers, and third-party representatives' to file in CCMS, so labs and consultancies who file on behalf of clients are a natural per-seat customer.
input: The customer's own model master plus their own certified test values, exactly the data they already hold: brand, basic model number, individual model numbers, product/equipment class, and the measured metric(s) from their accredited lab's test report (kWh/yr, EER/SEER2/CEER, AFUE, UEF, gpm, airflow/W, etc.), plus test sample size and whether an AEDM was used. Accepted as CSV/XLSX upload or by parsing the lab's report; the same file is reused every year with only changed rows edited. Friction is low because the customer must already assemble this to fill DOE's blank template by hand. No PHI, no PII, no consumer data, no bank or payroll connection — the only sensitive content is pre-market model data, so the product ships with per-tenant isolation and an explicit 'we never publish your models' guarantee. corpus: Every source fetched live today, 2026-08-20, with byte counts.
