kill_checks: Pattern 1 — free first-party substitute. Checked and survived, with the exact boundary documented. FTC's own manufacturer templates page (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/energyguide-labels-templates-manufacturers, fetched today, 992,593 bytes) ships ~26 BLANK Adobe Illustrator .ai and .eps artboards and instructs: 'Insert the correct energy, cost, range, and any other model-specific information for your particular model on the labels. Place the cost of your product at the appropriate location along the range,' and warns 'The label files on this page provide example templates to facilitate label design but do not cover every possible product type or size.' That is a blank artboard, not a generator: it computes nothing and requires Illustrator. DOE likewise ships blank product-specific Excel certification templates plus a free CCMS upload portal (https://www.regulations.doe.gov/ccms/templates, HTTP 200 today) — again a form, not a generator. The one calculator DOE does host is a consumer ZIP-code energy-cost estimator (zipdata.csv fetched today, ZIP-level electricprice 0.143 for ZIP 01001) which uses different inputs from the label's codified Appendix K1 figure ($0.1400/kWh flat), so it cannot produce a compliant label value. No free agency generator exists. Free VALIDATION does exist (CCMS runs template validations on upload) and that is fine — validators are allowed; generators are not, and there is none. Pattern 2 — live micro-SaaS incumbents. Two independent searches today ('EnergyGuide label generator software ... pricing' and 'EnergyGuide label software service create labels ... Amazon requires energy guide label') returned no third-party generator product; the search engine explicitly reported 'I did not find a specific third-party software service that automatically creates EnergyGuide labels' and 'The FTC primarily provides free templates for manufacturers to create their own labels.' The only vendors surfacing are Intertek, selling EnergyGuide LAB TESTING as a service (https://www.intertek.com/appliances/energy-efficiency/america/energyguide/), and Doxcelerate, which is DOE's own CCMS build contractor (www2.doxcelerate.com/products/ccms/) and sells to the agency, not to filers. I could not find a published incumbent price, which is a real gap — recorded honestly under risks, not papered over. Pattern 3 — bundling. Nothing the buyer already pays for does this. Searches for CCMS/certification software and for label software surfaced no PLM, ERP, PIM, artwork-management or e-commerce product that performs 16 CFR 305 arithmetic or maps a model list into DOE's product-class templates. Test labs perform it as a paid human service, which is the consultant incumbent, not a bundle. Pattern 4 — premise. Verified verbatim against primary text fetched today, quoted above: 10 CFR 429.12(a) 'and annually thereafter'; 16 CFR 305.11(a)(1) 'shall submit annually a report for each model in current production'; 305.11(b)(1) Table 1 per-category deadlines; 305.12(a)-(b) the 2027 revision with its 90-day conformance clock. The agency publishes the tables and the deadlines; it does not compute the customer's numbers or draw the customer's label. Pattern 5 — A4 / fifty-jurisdiction conflict. Does not apply. One federal jurisdiction, two CFR titles, one machine-readable API (eCFR versioner JSON/XML) that returns the appendices as structured tables. No prose extraction across states, no scraper fleet. The optional California CEC MAEDbS output is one additional jurisdiction, deliberately deferred to a later tier, not fifty. Pattern 6 — dead data. Every source was fetched today with a non-trivial byte count and current content: eCFR part 305 264,014 bytes at the 2026-08-01 point-in-time, 10 CFR 429.12 13,449 bytes, title-16 structure 754,206 bytes, DOE zipdata.csv 1,352,949 bytes, Federal Register API newest FTC hit 2026-08-14 and newest DOE hit 2026-07-07. DOE's own database page states a two-week refresh cadence, which gives a testable staleness expectation. Nothing here has live-looking metadata over dead rows. Pattern 7 — engine never arbiter. The product never asserts that a model complies. It performs published arithmetic on the customer's own certified test values and prints, beside every field, the CFR citation and the input it came from. The compliance statement that actually carries liability is the one 10 CFR 429.12(c) requires a named company official to sign — the customer signs it, in their own CCMS account, and the product says so permanently in-product. The genuinely ambiguous case is prescribed by the rule itself rather than by us: when a model's cost falls outside the current published range, 16 CFR 305.12(c) dictates omitting the marker and adding a specific sentence, so the engine follows the regulation instead of judging. Where a product class has no template match, or a test value is missing or out of unit range, the model is parked in a visible 'cannot generate — N models' bucket, excluded from any completeness claim, and never silently filled with a guess.
evidence: The strongest evidence is the regulator's own dollar figure for the labor this replaces, fetched today. DOE's PRA notice at 89 FR 80235 (published 2024-10-02, full text fetched 2026-08-20): 'Annual Estimated Number of Respondents: 2,083; Annual Estimated Number of Total Responses: 32,243; Annual Estimated Number of Burden Hours: 775,965 (35 hours per certification ...)' and 'Annual Estimated Reporting and Recordkeeping Cost Burden: $56,645,445.00' — $56.6M a year, ~$27,193 per obligated company per year, for producing exactly this artifact by hand. FTC's parallel PRA notice (88 FR 84330, published 2023-12-05, fetched today) supplies the model base and the honest counterweight: 'Based on Department of Energy data, staff has estimated that manufacturers offer approximately 69,676 basic models of covered products' and 'manufacturers draft or revise labels for 25% of the total basic models each year' — ~17,400 labels regenerated annually — while pricing label drafting at only four minutes per model, i.e. ~1,161 hours and roughly $22k of national labor a year. The successor notice (89 FR 13719, 2024-02-23, fetched today) totals the Energy Labeling Rule at 821,651 hours and $24,690,012 labor plus $3,000,000 non-labor. Read together these say plainly: the LABEL half is a wedge worth a few tens of thousands of dollars of national labor, and the DOE CERTIFICATION half is the $56.6M business. Third-party money already changing hands for a worse solution: Intertek sells EnergyGuide work as a lab/consulting engagement (https://www.intertek.com/appliances/energy-efficiency/america/energyguide/), and DOE's CCMS explicitly contemplates 'third-party representatives' filing on manufacturers' behalf — a paid human service. What I could NOT prove today: no incumbent published a per-label or per-certification price on any page I fetched, and the Amazon Seller Central threads about EnergyGuide label restrictions require login and were not fetched. Both are recorded as unproven rather than asserted.
pricing_hypothesis: Anchored to DOE's own $27,193 per respondent per year, not to a competitor's page (there isn't one). $249/mo Importer — up to 25 basic models in one product class, annual DOE certification report file, EnergyGuide label artwork and web image, hosted label URL to satisfy 16 CFR 305.9 and 305.11(a)(5). $749/mo Manufacturer — up to 250 basic models, all product and equipment classes, per-category deadline calendar driven off 16 CFR 305.11(b)(1) Table 1, template-version and eCFR change watch with a diff of what moved and which of your models it touches, dated artifact archive. $1,999/mo Portfolio / Third-Party Representative — unlimited models, multi-client workspaces for labs and consultancies filing on behalf of manufacturers, API, California CEC MAEDbS output as it lands. Annual prepay at -20%. A one-time '2027 Range Revision Regeneration' package sold when FTC publishes the revised ranges, priced per model, is the natural burst offer against the 90-day conformance clock in 16 CFR 305.12(a). Every tier is self-serve Stripe Checkout; the $1,999 tier is still self-serve because the customer's own CCMS credentials never touch us.
moat: Three layers, one of which cannot be back-filled. (1) The class-to-template-to-appendix map: which of DOE's 65+ product and equipment classes uses which current CCMS template version, which required field set from 10 CFR 429.14-429.63, which rounding rule from 10 CFR 429/430, and which comparability-range appendix and Representative Average Unit Energy Cost from 16 CFR 305 — an encoding nobody publishes as a single machine object, assembled from two CFR titles and DOE's template library. (2) A dated archive of every DOE template version and every eCFR revision of parts 429/430/431 and 16 CFR 305, accumulated from day one. DOE publishes only the CURRENT templates and eCFR serves point-in-time text but no per-appendix changelog, so 'what was the correct label and the correct report for this model on this date' — the exact question an enforcement action or a retailer audit asks — becomes answerable only for someone who has been snapshotting. A competitor starting later cannot recreate it retroactively. (3) The customer's own model-and-test-value master, re-used every year across a growing model count, which makes churn cost a re-keying project rather than a cancel button. The 2027 range revision is a one-time land-grab on top: whoever can regenerate 69,676 basic models' worth of labels inside a 90-day window owns the moment.
risks: NOT YET PROVEN, in order of how badly it could break the thesis. (1) No incumbent price was found today for per-label or per-certification service work, so willingness to pay rests on DOE's PRA cost figure rather than on an observed transaction — the first build-phase task is to obtain a quote from a lab or regulatory consultancy for preparing one certification report and one EnergyGuide label, and to fetch it. (2) The buyer count is small: 2,083 respondents by DOE's count. This is a high-ACV, low-count business, not a $49/mo long tail; if the real self-serve segment is only the importer slice, the reachable count may be a few hundred. Self-serve conversion at a $749-1,999/mo ACV is unproven. (3) FTC's own PRA prices label drafting at four minutes a model, which means the LABEL story will not carry the sale on its own — the DOE annual certification report has to be the headline or the offer reads as a $30 nice-to-have. (4) Amazon/retailer enforcement pain is the emotional trigger and it is currently sourced only from search snippets of login-walled Seller Central threads; it must be verified from a fetchable source before it appears in any marketing copy. (5) Template drift: DOE revises certification templates and did so materially in the 2024-10-09 and 2025-09-09 certification final rules; if the template-version watch lags, the product emits a file CCMS rejects. Mitigation is the weekly template check plus fail-closed generation, but it is real maintenance. (6) Scope creep into arbiter territory: customers will ask 'am I compliant', 'is my AEDM defensible', 'which basic models can I group' — 429.7 basic-model grouping is a genuine judgment call and must be refused in-product with a citation, not answered. (7) A lab or a certification body (Intertek, UL, CSA) could productise this as a free add-on to testing; the defence is that they sell hours and this sells files, plus the dated archive. (8) The 2027 range revision is a dated opportunity but also a dependency — if FTC slips the revision, the burst revenue slips with it, so the base subscription must stand alone on the annual certification cycle.

name: NinetyEight
one_liner: Generates the CFR-prescribed Chapter 98 claim package — the foreign repairer's / assembler's / shipper's declaration, the importer's endorsement, and the itemized value schedule behind it — from the customer's own outbound-export and inbound-invoice CSVs, so the new 10–12.5% Section 301 duty is assessed on the repair or assembly value instead of the full value of the returning article.
artifact: Per inbound shipment (or per blanket period), a signable PDF package plus a broker-keyable CSV of entry-line values. Three artifact families, each with its wording fixed verbatim by regulation and each fetched today from eCFR: (1) 9802.00.40/.50 repairs & alterations — the '19 CFR 10.8(a)(1)' declaration by the person who performed the repairs (columns: Marks and numbers | Description of articles and of repairs or alterations | Full cost or (when no charge is made) value of repairs or alterations | Total value of articles after repairs or alterations) plus the 10.8(a)(2) declaration by the owner/importer naming the port and date of export and asserting no drawback; (2) 9802.00.80 US components assembled abroad — the 19 CFR 10.24(a)(1) Declaration by the Assembler (columns: Marks of identification, numbers | Description of component | Quantity | Unit value at time and place of export from United States | Port and date of export from United States | Name and address of manufacturer) plus the 10.24(a)(2) importer endorsement, plus the free-text description of operations performed abroad which the CUSTOMER writes and we only place; (3) 9801.00.10 American Goods Returned over $2,500 — the 19 CFR 10.1(a)(1) foreign shipper's declaration (Marks | Number | Quantity | Description | Value in U.S. coin) plus the 10.1(a)(2) owner/importer declaration. Each package also carries a dutiable-value worksheet (entered value; deducted US-component or original value; remaining base; duty at the chapter-99 and chapter-1-97 rates read from the live HTS API on the date of generation; dollars saved vs. full-value entry) and the 5-year retention bundle that 19 CFR 10.24(d) demands (quantities, sources, costs, dates shipped abroad). Cadence: per shipment for RMA/repair flows (weekly for a depot-repair operation); blanket component lists regenerated per 10.24(c)/(d) as BOMs change.
mandate: Primary text, all fetched 2026-08-20. (a) 19 CFR 10.8(a) — 'the following documents shall be filed in connection with the entry of articles which are returned after having been exported for repairs or alterations and which are claimed to be subject to duty only on the value of the repairs or alterations performed abroad under subheading 9802.00.40 or 9802.00.50' — and it then PRINTS the required wording (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-01/title-19.xml?part=10&section=10.8). (b) 19 CFR 10.24(a) — same construction for 9802.00.80, printing the assembler's declaration table and the importer's endorsement. (c) 19 CFR 10.1(a) — same for 9801.00.10/9802.00.20 shipments over $2,500. Title 19 reports latest_amended_on 2026-08-12, up_to_date_as_of 2026-08-18 (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/titles.json, fetched 2026-08-20). WHO MUST FILE: the importer of record claiming the partial-duty subheading; the declaration itself must be signed by the foreign repairer/assembler/shipper and endorsed by the importer. WHEN: in connection with each entry (or by reference to previously approved blanket lists under 10.24(c)). PENALTY: no filing fine — the sanction is denial. Without the declarations and value documentation CBP assesses duty on the FULL value of the article, and a claim asserted without support is a 19 U.S.C. 1592 false-statement exposure. THE DOLLAR STAKE IS NEW: USTR's Notice of Actions (published 2026-07-28; text fetched from https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2026/07/28/2026-15181.txt) imposes Section 301 duties of 10% on goods of Canada, Mexico, India, the UK, Indonesia, Malaysia and 11 other economies and 12.5% on the rest of 60 investigated economies, and its new HTSUS U.S. note 52(a) states verbatim: 'The additional duties imposed by headings 9903.05.20-9903.05.84 shall not apply to goods for which entry is properly claimed under a provision of chapter 98 of the tariff schedule ... except for goods entered under subheadings 9802.00.40, 9802.00.50 or 9802.00.60 or heading 9802.00.80. For goods entered under subheadings 9802.00.40, 9802.00.50 and 9802.00.60, the additional duties apply to the value of repairs, alterations or processing performed, as described in the applicable subheading. For goods entered under heading 9802.00.80, the additional duties apply to the value of the article assembled abroad, less the cost or value of such products of the United States.' So the new duty is computed on the reduced Chapter 98 base — but only for an importer who can produce the declarations.
buyer: US importers of record with a recurring cross-border return leg: (a) depot-repair / RMA / warranty-return operations (industrial equipment, medical devices, semiconductors capital equipment, avionics, instruments) that ship a unit abroad for repair and bring it back; (b) manufacturers assembling abroad from US-fabricated components; (c) companies re-importing US-origin goods (trade-show, rental fleet, e-commerce returns from abroad). Reachable self-serve because the buyer is a trade-compliance manager or ops/finance lead at a 20–500 person importer, and the entry point is a CSV upload, not an integration. HONEST GAP: I could not size this set from a primary source today. api.census.gov/data/timeseries/intltrade/imports/hs returned HTTP 302 (key required) for a 9802 query, and USITC DataWeb is token-gated, so the count of US importers filing 9802/9801 claims is NOT established and must be pulled from DataWeb or a FOIA'd CBP entry-line count before any build decision.
input: Two CSVs the customer already possesses. (1) The outbound export record per part: part number, description, quantity, unit value at time and place of export, port and date of export, US manufacturer name and address (exactly the 10.24 columns). (2) The inbound foreign invoice: repair/alteration/assembly charges, labour and parts split, quantity returned, and the customer's own one-paragraph description of the operation performed abroad. Optionally the ACE/entry-summary export for reconciliation. Friction is low-to-medium: the export leg data lives in the customer's ERP shipment records; the hardest field is the US manufacturer name for older components, which the product surfaces as a named gap rather than filling. NO PHI, NO PII — commercial part and value data only; the parser rejects any column that looks like a person's identifiers other than the signatory block.

(6) DEAD DATA — checked both feeds by content, not metadata: eCFR title 19 reports latest_amended_on 2026-08-12 AND returned live section bodies today; HTS reststop reports currentRelease 2026HTSRev16 AND returned live 9802/9903 rows with current duty language today. Neither is a live-looking-metadata-over-dead-rows case. (7) ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER — this is the design constraint, not an afterthought. The engine never decides whether an operation is an 'alteration' rather than a manufacture, never decides whether components were 'exported in condition ready for assembly without further fabrication', never asserts that a claim will be allowed. The customer writes the operation description; the engine places it into the CFR's own wording. The engine's arithmetic is limited to summing customer-supplied component values, subtracting them from the customer-supplied entered value, and multiplying by a rate read live from the HTS API — every input is shown on the worksheet next to its source. The declarations are signed by the foreign party and the importer; our name appears nowhere on them. WHAT FREE AGENCY TOOLING EXISTS AND WHY THE PRODUCT SURVIVES IT: the government gives away the RULE (eCFR) and third parties give away the BLANK (Livingston, Deringer). Nobody gives away the filled artifact built from the customer's export ledger, the per-component value schedule with port and date of export, the duty-saved arithmetic, or the 10.24(d) five-year retention bundle — which is the same shape as run 2's winner, where the WH-347 blank was also free and the generation from the customer's CSV against a public corpus was not.
evidence: Money already changing hands for a worse solution, all fetched 2026-08-20: (a) Kendrick Trade charges $499–$999/mo for exactly the adjacent job — 'generate my mandatory trade artifact from my own BOM' — proving SMB trade teams pay four figures monthly for artifact generation rather than advice (https://www.kendricktrade.com/pricing); its $249.99–$999.99/mo document-solicitation line proves they also pay to chase a foreign counterparty for a signed compliance document, which is the 10.8/10.24 signature loop. (c) Every enterprise alternative that does cover Chapter 98 is quote-only with 12–14 week implementations (https://www.freehand.ai/articles/best-fta-qualification-software), i.e. structurally unavailable to the 20–500 person importer. (d) The pain is documented by practitioners: AAEI's Chapter 98 piece (https://aaei.org/chapter-98-tariff-saving-strategies/, fetched 2026-08-20) names 'missing documentation — filing claims without robust supporting evidence' and 'waiting until after importation' as the top failure modes and stresses that the importer bears the burden of proof. WEAKEST LINK, STATED PLAINLY: I did NOT find a fetched price for a consultant doing a 9802 program specifically. General trade/compliance consulting rates of $150–$400/hr appear on consultfees.com and ziprecruiter (surfaced 2026-08-19/20) but those are secondary aggregators, not a quote for this work, and I am not treating them as evidence.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo Starter (25 packages/yr, one subheading family, PDF + broker CSV) → $299/mo Operating (300 packages/yr, all of 9801.00.10 / 9802.00.40 / .50 / .80, blanket component lists, retention bundle, duty-saved reporting) → $799/mo Multi-entity (unlimited packages, multiple importer-of-record entities, API, per-part US-content ledger export). moat: Thin on day one and I will not overclaim it. The only durable asset is the accumulating per-part US-content and export-provenance ledger that 19 CFR 10.24(d) itself requires — 'records of United States components showing quantities, sources, costs, dates shipped abroad ... maintained by the importer and assembler for 5 years' — because a customer who has run the product for two years holds a dated, contemporaneous history that a competitor cannot retro-create and that is exactly the record CBP asks for on audit. Secondary and weaker: a maintained mapping of chapter-99 action → whether it applies to the full or the reduced Chapter 98 base, versioned as new proclamations land (note 52(a) is one such mapping; there will be more). risks: NOT YET PROVEN, in order of severity. (1) Buyer count is unsized: the Census intltrade API returned HTTP 302 (key required) for a 9802 query today and USITC DataWeb is token-gated, so I have NO primary figure for how many importers file 9801/9802 claims or for the annual value entered under them. (2) The free blank templates (Livingston, Deringer, both fetched) mean the buyer's first instinct is 'the form is free' — the whole sale rests on the value schedule, the arithmetic and the retention bundle carrying the weight, and that has not been tested on a real buyer. (5) Eligibility is ruling-driven ('alteration' vs manufacture; 'ready for assembly without further fabrication'), so the engine must decline to opine, which caps the promise to 'your package, computed and rendered' rather than 'your claim will be allowed' — a weaker headline than a qualification engine. (6) The foreign party must sign; that is a solicitation loop the customer runs, and Kendrick already sells document solicitation at $249.99/mo and could extend into Chapter 98 declarations with modest effort — this is the most likely competitive incursion. If it falls, the incremental dollar stake shrinks to the MFN duty on the deducted value, which is real but far smaller. (8) 9802.00.50's Special column already shows Free for a list of FTA partners, so for some origins the deduction is worth less than the headline — the worksheet must read the actual Special rate per origin rather than assume the general rate.

name: Addendum
one_liner: Turns a NYC property owner's existing rent-roll and P&L exports into the NYC Department of Finance's own mandatory RPIE rent roll addendum spreadsheet, storefront registry rows and completed RPIE worksheet — per BBL, in the exact DOF-published column spec, entirely in the browser so tenant data never leaves the customer's machine.
artifact: Three generated files per BBL per filing season, all in formats DOF itself publishes but does not generate for you: (1) the DOF Rent Roll Addendum workbook — the ONLY accepted upload format ('You must use the rent roll spreadsheet provided by the Department of Finance... This is the only version you will be able to upload', nyc.gov/site/finance/property/property-rpie-rent-roll.page, fetched 2026-08-20) — with the commercial tab populated across columns A,E–AD and the residential tab across A,E–U per DOF's own rent-roll-column-definitions.pdf (fetched 2026-08-20, 2 pages, full column list extracted); (2) a completed RPIE worksheet mirroring DOF's RPIE-2025 WORKSHEET (nyc.gov/assets/finance/downloads/pdf/rpie/rpie-worksheet.pdf, 'Revised 3.2.2026', 27 pages, HTTP 200 950KB fetched 2026-08-20) Sections I/J/K income lines 1–12, operating-expense lines and Section E vacancy — the keying script for SmartFile; (3) Section S storefront registration rows (DOF permits 'up to 200 storefronts for your property and up to 24 occupancies for each storefront', same worksheet p.11). Cadence: annual RPIE + storefront deadline June 1; storefront supplemental registrations August 15 and February 15 (nyc.gov/site/finance/property/storefront-registry-requirement.page, fetched 2026-08-20). Channel: browser upload in, ZIP of DOF-format files out; the owner uploads the rent roll workbook to DOF SmartFile and certifies.
mandate: NYC Department of Finance, RPIE-2025 Worksheet and Instructions (nyc.gov/assets/finance/downloads/pdf/rpie/rpie-worksheet.pdf, revised 3.2.2026, fetched 2026-08-20), text extracted verbatim: 'Owners of income-producing properties with an Actual Assessed Value of more than $40,000 as stated on the 2026-2027 Tentative Assessment Roll are required to file Real Property Income and Expense statements ("RPIE") or a Claim of Exclusion annually with the Department of Finance'; 'The submission deadline for all RPIE filings is June 1, 2026'; 'All filers are legally required to file electronically unless Finance grants a waiver.' Exclusions enumerated in the same document: AV of $40,000 or less; residential properties with 10 or fewer dwelling units; tax class 1 or 2 with six or fewer dwelling units and no more than one commercial unit; special franchise properties. Rent roll addendum: 'RPIE filers whose properties have an actual assessed value of $750,000 or greater are required to file an addendum containing rent roll information' (nyc.gov/site/finance/property/property-rpie-rent-roll.page, fetched 2026-08-20). Penalty schedule, quoted from DOF's own page (nyc.gov/site/finance/property/property-rpie.page, fetched 2026-08-20): $40,001–$99,999 = $300; $100,000–$249,999 = $750; $250,000–$499,999 = $1,500; $500,000–$999,999 = $3,000; $1,000,000–$4,999,999 = $5,000; $5,000,000–$9,999,999 = $20,000; $10,000,000–$14,999,999 = $40,000; $15,000,000–$24,999,999 = $60,000; $25,000,000+ = $100,000; plus '$100 the first year' for a missing claim of exclusion. Storefront registry authority: 'Local Law 157 of 2019, amended in 2022' (storefront-registry-requirement.page, fetched 2026-08-20). SSN/EIN collection authority cited by DOF is Administrative Code §11-102.1 (worksheet p.2).
buyer: NYC owners and managing agents of tax-class-2 and tax-class-4 income-producing property, and the small CPA/bookkeeping firms that file for them. Counts computed live today (2026-08-20) against NYC Open Data's Property Valuation and Assessment Data dataset 8y4t-faws via the Socrata API, not from memory: 63,402 non-condo-unit TC2/TC4 parcels on the 2026 final roll carry actual AV >= $750,000 and therefore owe the rent roll addendum; of those, 31,585 have NO tax-certiorari attorney of record in DOF's own attorney_group1 field — the unbundled core. Widening to AV > $40,000 (RPIE due, addendum not): 382,868 TC2/TC4 parcels, of which 119,069 are non-condo-unit AND have no attorney of record. Self-serve reachable because the buyer is already logging into DOF SmartFile with an NYC.ID themselves; there is no gatekeeper, no license, no procurement — the transaction is 'give me the file I have to upload'. input: Three files the customer already produces: (a) a rent roll export from Yardi / MRI / AppFolio / Buildium / RealPage or plain Excel; (b) a per-property P&L or trial balance export (QuickBooks class-based, Yardi GL, or CSV); (c) a list of BBLs. kill_checks: P1 FREE FIRST-PARTY SUBSTITUTE — checked, survives with a caveat. DOF publishes the filing portal (SmartFile, NYC.ID login), a BLANK rent roll template, blank worksheets and column definitions. DOF's own user guide describes the flow as 'you will be able to download a template, enter your information, and upload it' (rpie-statement-online-filing-user-guide.pdf Step 12, fetched 2026-08-20). That is a blank form plus a validator on submit — DOF publishes the SPEC and does not publish a CONVERTER from an owner's rent roll or GL export into it, and the guide documents no bulk or multi-property path: every BBL is a separate NYC.ID session. Same shape as the run-2 winner (agency publishes the filing spec, ships no generator). Caveat recorded honestly: the blank template lowers the ceiling for a 1-BBL owner; the product's value scales with BBL count and with the AV>=$750k addendum. P2 LIVE MICRO-SAAS INCUMBENTS — four searches (2026-08-20) for RPIE software/self-serve/automation surfaced ZERO self-serve products. Every provider found is human-prepared: nyrets.com/services/rpie-statement-preparation/ (fetched 2026-08-20 — 'every case is handled directly by our experienced team', no price published, contact form only); rltyservice.com (fetched 2026-08-20 — 'Full-service RPIE compliance, handled end-to-end', prices 'No filing, no fee' with the actual per-filing cost withheld, phone/email required); brooklyncpa.com, rpienyc.com, and tax-cert law firms. This is precisely the 'incumbents are human consultants' condition. P3 BUNDLING — checked and quantified rather than asserted. Two bundling channels exist. (a) Tax-certiorari counsel, who often file RPIE inside a contingency cert engagement: measured directly from DOF's own attorney_group1 field on the 2026 final roll today — 39,307 of 73,380 AV>=$750k TC2/4 parcels have an attorney of record, leaving 31,585 non-condo parcels unbundled. So bundling is real and covers roughly half the top band; the product is sold into the measured other half. (b) Property-management software: a targeted search (Yardi/MRI/AppFolio + RPIE + DOF format, 2026-08-20) returned no evidence of a native DOF rent-roll-addendum export from any of them; recorded as NOT FOUND rather than as proven absent. P4 PREMISE VS PRIMARY TEXT — verified against DOF's own instruction document and penalty page, quoted verbatim in the mandate field, including the exclusion list that shrinks the market (10-or-fewer dwelling units, AV<=$40,000). The agency does not compute the number: DOF collects the owner's income, expense and lease data precisely because it does not have it. P5 A4 CONFLICT — none. ONE jurisdiction, ONE agency, ONE published column spec of ~30 columns. No 50-state prose extraction, no scraper fleet; the only 'scraping' is three PDF hashes and one Socrata API. P6 DEAD DATA — checked, alive. 8y4t-faws rowsUpdatedAt resolves to 2026-06-15 and the 2027 roll year is materially present (1,180,360 rows, period 3), not a live-looking timestamp over frozen rows: I queried the 2027 rows themselves and got real counts (389,280 TC2/4 parcels AV>$40k). The DOF worksheet self-dates 'Revised 3.2.2026'. P7 ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER — the product emits files, never a filing. It signs nothing: the owner certifies in SmartFile. Its one numeric output is penalty exposure, and that is DOF's own published band table applied to DOF's own published assessed value — arithmetic on two agency numbers, shown with both cited. Any rent-roll row or GL account it cannot map lands in a visible 'Unmapped — N rows' bucket, is excluded from the emitted file, and is never guessed; the product never decides whether a lot qualifies for the exclusion, it shows DOF's four exclusion criteria against the roll fields and lets the owner answer.
evidence: Money is already changing hands for a strictly worse (human, slow, unpriced) version of this exact job: NYRETS sells 'Real Property Income and Expense (RPIE) Statement Preparation Services' as a hand-worked engagement with no published price (https://nyrets.com/services/rpie-statement-preparation/, fetched 2026-08-20); RLTY Service sells 'Full-service RPIE compliance, handled end-to-end' explicitly covering the 'Rent roll addendum (29-column DOF format)', 'Storefront registry filings (Local Law 157)' and 'Penalty dispute and appeal assistance', priced 'No filing, no fee' with the number withheld behind a phone call (https://rltyservice.com/, fetched 2026-08-20); Brooklyn CPA lists RPIE statements as a billed service line (https://brooklyncpa.com/services/real-property-income-and-expense-statements-rpie-statements/, surfaced 2026-08-20); national accounting and cert firms publish RPIE advisory content as practice marketing (Anchin, Citrin Cooperman, EisnerAmper, Rosenberg & Estis, all surfaced 2026-08-20). The downside the buyer is paying to avoid is a published dollar figure, not a vibe: DOF's own penalty table runs $300 to $100,000 per property per year by assessed-value band (https://www.nyc.gov/site/finance/property/property-rpie.page, fetched 2026-08-20), and a mid-market $1M–$5M AV building faces $5,000 for one missed filing. HONEST GAP: not one incumbent publishes a price. I could not fetch a single dollar figure charged for RPIE preparation. Willingness to pay is inferred from (a) the existence of at least four distinct paid human services, (b) the penalty schedule, and (c) the measured 31,585 unbundled AV>=$750k parcels — it is NOT proven by a fetched price, and that is the first thing to test.
pricing_hypothesis: Per-BBL, per-filing-season, self-serve Stripe checkout. $79/BBL for RPIE worksheet + Section S storefront rows (AV $40,001–$749,999). $199/BBL where the rent roll addendum is required (AV >= $750,000) — the band where the hand-keying is worst and where DOF's 30-column workbook is mandatory. Portfolio: $1,200 for 10 BBLs, $3,900 for 40 BBLs, $8,500 for 150 BBLs (managing agents and small CPA firms). Free forever: the penalty-exposure sheet — paste BBLs, get each one's DOF assessed value, DOF penalty band, whether the addendum threshold is crossed, and whether an attorney of record is on the roll. That freebie is pure agency arithmetic, costs nothing to serve, is the SEO and email-capture surface, and is honest about doing nothing more than reading DOF's own two numbers. Anchor: $199 is ~4% of the $5,000 penalty a $1M–$5M AV building faces for one missed year, and undercuts any hand-prepared engagement that requires a phone call.
moat: Three layers, only one of which is code. (1) The mapping library: the column-shape fingerprints of real Yardi, MRI, AppFolio, Buildium, RealPage and hand-rolled Excel rent rolls and GLs, mapped onto DOF's exact column spec, accumulated one customer at a time and reused across every customer on the same system — a new entrant starts from the blank DOF template with no fingerprints. (2) A dated archive of every season's DOF template version, column definition PDF and worksheet, hashed on capture, plus a snapshot of each tentative and final assessment roll — which lets the product reconcile this year's filing against last year's numbers (DOF cross-checks year-over-year) and answer 'what did the spec say when we filed in 2027'. Nobody can backfill that after the fact; DOF replaces its PDFs in place. (3) The client-side-only architecture, which is a structural rather than feature moat: an incumbent human service or a server-side clone cannot claim 'we never receive your tenant SSNs', and that claim is what gets the product past an owner's counsel.
risks: SEASONALITY IS THE BIGGEST FLAW AND IT IS STRUCTURAL. The RPIE-2025 deadline was June 1, 2026 — already past. The next full season is RPIE-2026, forms typically posted around February with a June 1, 2027 deadline, i.e. roughly six months of dead air from today. The only nearer revenue events are the storefront supplemental registration due February 15, 2027 and off-season amended filings and DOF penalty notices. Any factory expecting revenue in weeks should treat this as disqualifying; a factory willing to build against a dated calendar gets an unusually well-specified target. NOT YET PROVEN: (a) no incumbent price was obtainable, so the $79/$199 hypothesis is unanchored on the demand side; (b) no evidence was found either way on whether Yardi/MRI/AppFolio ship a DOF rent-roll export — searched, not found, must be confirmed by asking three managing agents before building; (c) I did not fetch the actual Administrative Code §11-208.1 text (amlegal, Stewart and public.law all returned 403/404 today) and am relying on DOF's own instruction PDF and penalty page as the primary agency statement — the code section should be read from a fetchable source before any marketing copy cites it. OTHER RISKS: DOF could ship its own converter or a bulk multi-property path at any time and hollow the product out overnight; roughly half the AV>=$750k band already sits with a cert attorney who may absorb the work for free; the RPIE body itself still has to be keyed into SmartFile by hand because only the rent roll and lease accept upload, so the product removes most but not all of the labour; the rent roll contains residential tenant names and commercial tenant SSNs, so the browser-only transform is not a nice-to-have but a load-bearing requirement, and any drift toward server-side processing turns this into a data-breach liability; and the buyer population skews old-school NYC real estate, where the default answer is 'my accountant does it'.

name: Filing Period
one_liner: Turns one accounts-payable CSV export into the complete statutory UK payment practices report — every count, value and construction-retention field in DBT's 52-field published spec, plus the invoice-level workbook showing how each number was derived — inside the 30-day statutory filing period whose breach is a criminal offence for the company and every director.
artifact: Per qualifying company (or LLP) per reporting period, three deterministic outputs from one AP ledger export: (1) SUBMISSION PACK — every field of the statutory report, field-for-field in the order the GOV.UK publish service asks for them, so the finance manager keys or pastes it in one sitting: average time to pay; % of payments made in 0-30 / 31-60 / 61+ days; % not paid within agreed terms; % late due to dispute; total number of payments; the value-based statistics mandatory for financial years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2025 (sum of payments in each speed band, sum not paid within agreed terms); the construction retention block mandatory from 1 Mar 2025 (retention-vs-client ratio (Sum A / Sum B) x 100, retention as % of gross payments (Sum C / Sum D) x 100, plus the retention narrative and tick-box statements); and the persisted narrative/tick-box answers (standard terms, changes and supplier notification, dispute resolution process, e-invoicing, supply-chain finance, supplier-list charges, payment-code membership, approving director's name). (2) DERIVATION WORKBOOK — one row per invoice and per payment showing which date field was used as the receipt date, which exclusion rule (financial services / residential occupier / intra-entity / fully credit-noted / not a qualifying contract) fired, which speed band it landed in, and the running arithmetic behind each headline statistic. This is the reg 9 defence artifact. (3) DIRECTORS' REPORT PAYMENT BLOCK — the six payment data elements for the statutory directors' report, elements 4-6 (the sum-based ones) applying to financial years starting on or after 1 Jan 2026, generated from the same source rows so the two published artifacts cannot disagree. CADENCE: twice per financial year per qualifying entity, publishable only inside the 30-day filing period. CHANNEL: customer downloads the pack and publishes it themselves on publish-payment-practices.service.gov.uk. We never file, never sign, never assert; the named director approves and publishes.
mandate: The Reporting on Payment Practices and Performance Regulations 2017 (SI 2017/395), fetched as-made from legislation.gov.uk 2026-08-20. Reg 2: "'filing period' means 30 days beginning with the day after the last day of the reporting period to which a report relates". Reg 8(1): "If the requirements of regulation 3 are not met in relation to a reporting period, the qualifying company and every person who was a director of the qualifying company immediately before the end of the filing period commits an offence"; reg 8(2) gives a director a defence only "to prove that the director took all reasonable steps"; reg 8(3) liability on summary conviction to a fine (England and Wales) / level 5 (Scotland, NI). Reg 9: separate offence for knowingly or recklessly publishing a report or information that is misleading, false or deceptive. Reg 6 defines qualifying contract (not financial services; UK-linked). WHO MUST FILE: from 6 April 2025, companies and LLPs exceeding 2 of 3 thresholds — £54m turnover, £27m balance sheet, 250 employees (DBT statutory guidance, updated 2 September 2025, fetched 2026-08-20). LLPs are covered by the parallel SI 2017/425. STILL LIVE AND EXTENDED: SI 2024/444 (fetched 2026-08-20) reg 2(2) replaces the 2017 sunset date "6th April 2024" with "6th April 2031", and reg 2(4) inserts Schedule para 9(c) (sum totals of payments in each band) and paras 10A/10B (value not paid within the payment period; % late as a result of a dispute), applying "in relation to each financial year of a company beginning on or after 1st January 2025". SI 2025/75 (fetched 2026-08-20) came into force 1 March 2025 and adds an entire new Schedule of retention-clause information for qualifying construction contracts (paras 2-12, including the contract-sum and retention definitions). The Companies (Directors' Report) (Payment Reporting) Regulations 2025 add a second, separate artifact: payment data inside the statutory directors' report, with the three sum-based elements applying to financial years starting on or after 1 January 2026 (DBT guidance published 30 December 2025, fetched 2026-08-20). WHEN: within 30 days of each of the two reporting periods per financial year. PENALTY: criminal, on the company and on every director personally.
buyer: UK qualifying companies and LLPs — mid-market finance teams (financial controller / finance manager / group reporting accountant), not enterprise GRC buyers. COUNT, SOURCED FROM THE REGULATOR'S OWN PUBLICATION REGISTER (full export CSV downloaded 2026-08-20, 102,349,420 bytes): 10,235 distinct company numbers have ever published a report; 6,340 distinct companies published at least one report between 1 Jan 2026 and 20 Aug 2026, across 10,762 reports. 3,762 of those 6,340 companies published 2 or more reports in 2026 — group structures where each qualifying subsidiary files separately, plus multi-period catch-ups. This is a bounded, finite, fully enumerable market: every buyer is named, with a company number, filing dates and prior published figures, in a free OGL-licensed CSV. SELF-SERVE REACHABLE BECAUSE: (a) the entire prospect list is public, so acquisition is programmatic — a free per-company benchmark page for all 10,235 companies (their published history vs their SIC-sector distribution, computed from the same corpus) is pure SEO against searches the finance manager already makes; (b) the trigger is calendar-fixed and knowable per entity from the corpus (period end + 30 days), so the outbound is a dated, entity-specific email with their own last-published numbers in it; (c) the purchase is a single finance manager's decision at £249-£899, below any procurement threshold; (d) 27.2% of 2026 reports were published after the 30-day filing period closed, so a quarter of the market self-identifies as struggling, by name, in public.
input: One accounts-payable ledger export per qualifying entity per reporting period, as CSV or XLSX: invoice reference, supplier reference, invoice receipt date (and, separately, invoice date and posting date so the product can show which it used), agreed payment period or terms code, gross invoice amount, payment date(s) and amount(s), credit note linkage, dispute flag, and a contract-class flag for the statutory exclusions and for construction contracts. Every named ERP and bookkeeping package the buyer segment runs exports these fields natively (Xero, QuickBooks, Sage 50/200/X3, NetSuite, Dynamics 365 F&O, SAP). FRICTION: low but not zero — one export per entity per period, plus a one-time settings pass where the customer states their exclusion rules, their receipt-date convention, their dispute-flag field and their narrative/tick-box answers; those persist and are reused every period, so period 2 onward is upload-and-download. Where the export lacks a true invoice-receipt date, the product does not guess: it names the substitute date field it used, on the face of the pack, and repeats that disclosure in the derivation workbook. NO PII/PHI TRAP: a purchase ledger is B2B entity data (supplier name, invoice, amount, dates). The uploader spec omits bank details and individual-person fields entirely, and the parser drops any column not in the declared schema rather than storing it. No employee data, no health data, no consumer data, no special-category data. Sole-trader supplier names are the only edge case; they are used solely as a row label and can be hashed at upload by a toggle that is on by default.

kill_checks: PATTERN 1 — FREE FIRST-PARTY SUBSTITUTE: PARTIAL HIT, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT KILLED THE PRIOR BALLOT. DBT ships, free: an eligibility checker (https://check-payment-practices.service.gov.uk/decide/, HTTP 200 today), a reporting-period-and-deadline calculator, a publication form, and a search/export of all reports. That is why any monitoring or deadline-reminder product in this space is dead on arrival — the government computes the deadline for you. What DBT does NOT ship, verified by fetching the guidance page (updated 2026-09-02) and the publish service landing page today: any calculator, any spreadsheet template, any file generator, and any bulk/CSV upload route. The publish service's own words, fetched 2026-08-20: "Once you've prepared all your report data, you must publish your report online." The regulator publishes the spec and prepares nothing. The only arithmetic the portal does is converting entered sums into percentages — confirmed empirically: across all 10,762 reports filed in 2026, zero have count-percentages that fail to sum to 100, because that division is done for you; every hard step (classifying invoices, counting days from receipt, applying reg 6 and the exclusion list, summing values, the two retention ratios) is not. CONTRAST WITH THE UK EPR CASE I KILLED THE SAME DAY: Defra publishes a free 'Packaging Data File Generator 2026' Excel tool that produces the submission CSV. DBT publishes no equivalent. PATTERN 2 — LIVE MICRO-SAAS INCUMBENTS: NOT FOUND, and I looked four ways — dedicated-tool search, SaaS/pricing-page search, G2/Capterra/Product Hunt search, and outsourced-service pricing search, all on 2026-08-20. No dedicated product, no published price, no directory listing. I am flagging the flip side honestly: absence of an incumbent price is also absence of proof that anyone pays for this as software (see risks). PATTERN 3 — BUNDLING: REAL, PARTIAL, AND THE SHARPEST RISK HERE. Two ERPs ship a UK payment practices helper report as standard localisation. Sage X3 (fetched 2026-08-20) requires the KUK localisation activity code and produces "average time to pay", the three count percentages, and the % not paid to terms. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance (doc dated 2026-05-12, fetched 2026-08-20) produces the same three statistics plus, since the 2024 Amendment Regulations, the total number of payments and the % late due to disputes, via ER configurations 'Statistics on payment practices (UK)' v67.18. WHY THE PRODUCT SURVIVES IT, from the vendors' own documentation rather than my assertion: (a) neither documents the VALUE-based statistics that the 2024 Regulations made mandatory for financial years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2025 — the sum totals per speed band and the sum not paid within terms; (b) neither documents any construction retention field from SI 2025/75, in force 1 March 2025; (c) neither produces the artifact — Sage X3's doc says "you need to manually enter the data on the UK government website", D365's says "use the report data to prepare the final report about payment practices for publication"; (d) neither produces the directors' report block; (e) both are the ERPs of only a slice of the segment — the corpus's 6,340 2026 filers include large numbers of £54m-turnover companies on Sage 50/200, Xero, QuickBooks and NetSuite with no such report at all. This is a partial hit, not a clean pass, and it is stated as the top risk. PATTERN 4 — PREMISE VS PRIMARY TEXT: VERIFIED CORRECT, not from commentary. I fetched SI 2017/395 as made and read reg 2 (30-day filing period), reg 8 (offence by the company AND every director, summary conviction fine, reasonable-steps defence) and reg 9 (false statement offence) in the statutory words. I fetched SI 2024/444 and confirmed reg 2(2) extends the regime's expiry from 6 April 2024 to 6 April 2031 — i.e. the obligation runs for at least another five years — and that reg 2(4) inserts the value metrics for financial years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2025. I fetched SI 2025/75 and confirmed it came into force 1 March 2025 with a whole new construction-retention Schedule. The regulator does NOT compute these numbers for the filer; it receives them and republishes them. PATTERN 5 — A4 / MULTI-JURISDICTION: CLEAN PASS. One jurisdiction, one regulator, one 52-field spec, one publication service, one statutory guidance document. No prose extraction across jurisdictions, no scraper fleet: the entire corpus is a single HTTP GET of one CSV, and the spec lives in four SIs and one guidance page. PATTERN 6 — DEAD DATA: DISPROVEN BY ROW-LEVEL FETCH, not metadata. I downloaded the whole 102MB register today and counted filings by month through to 478 in the first 20 days of August 2026 and 3,444 in July 2026, and confirmed 6,340 distinct companies filed in 2026. Rows are moving, not just metadata. PATTERN 7 — ENGINE NEVER ARBITER: PASS BY CONSTRUCTION, and reg 9 forces it. Every output number is arithmetic over the customer's own ledger rows against a published formula, shown with its lineage — the product never estimates, never scores, never predicts, never flags a named third party, and never claims the customer will or will not be prosecuted or excluded from a bid. Where a rule needs a fact only the customer holds (which contracts are financial services; which date is true receipt; which flag marks a dispute), the product refuses to choose: it presents the affected rows in an 'unresolved' bucket, excludes them from headline figures until the customer sets the rule once, and prints the choice on the face of the pack. A named director approves and publishes; we produce nothing that we sign.

A top-10 accountancy firm does not staff a service line for a job that takes ten minutes. Their price is quote-only; no figure is published, which I record as a gap rather than inflating it. (2) ERP VENDORS SPENDING ENGINEERING BUDGET. Microsoft maintained the UK payment practices localisation as recently as 2026-05-12 (doc date, fetched today), shipping updated ER configurations across four Dynamics 365 Finance release trains specifically to cover the 2024 Amendment Regulations; Sage ships an equivalent in X3 under the KUK localisation. Two ERP vendors funding recurring localisation work is proof the job is real, recurring and painful — and both stop at the same line, handing the user data and telling them to key the report themselves. (3) NON-COMPLIANCE MEASURED IN THE REGULATOR'S OWN REGISTER, COMPUTED BY ME TODAY from the 102MB export fetched 2026-08-20: of the 10,762 reports published between 1 Jan and 20 Aug 2026, 2,925 — 27.2% — were published more than 30 days after the end of the reporting period they cover. Under reg 8 that window closing is the moment the offence attaches to the company and to every director personally. Worked examples straight out of the file: ABCAM LIMITED, period ending 2025-06-30, published 2026-01-02, 186 days after period end; MABEY HIRE LIMITED, period ending 2025-09-01, published 2026-01-02, 123 days; BOYS & BODEN, LIMITED, period ending 2025-09-30, published 2026-01-02, 94 days. Over a quarter of this market is publicly, by name, missing a criminal-liability deadline. (4) THE SELF-EVIDENT DOWNSTREAM POUND FIGURE. Under PPN 018, applying to central government procurements above £5m per year advertised on or after 1 October 2025, a bidder's approach to payment is assessed at selection, with the average payment period threshold tightened from 55 to 45 days (PPN 015 having required 95% of invoices paid within 60 days and an average not exceeding 55). Computed today from the same corpus: 2,309 of the 10,044 reports with a parseable average-days figure filed in 2026 — 23.0% — show an average time to pay above 45 days, and 802 (8.0%) above 60 days. The number a company publishes in this report is the number that gates its eligibility for £5m+ public contracts, and once published it is permanent and public. That is the dollar answer the product hands the customer BEFORE they publish, computed from their own ledger: here is your average, here is the published threshold, here is the arithmetic. (5) DEMAND VOLUME: 10,762 reports published in 2026 to 20 August, 3,762 companies filing two or more, all inside a fixed 30-day window twice a year.
pricing_hypothesis: Per qualifying entity, per reporting period — the unit the law itself uses. £249 one-off per entity-report (upload, download the submission pack + derivation workbook; the trial-by-doing entry point, timed to a filing window). £99/month Single Entity (both reporting periods a year, directors' report payment block, persisted narrative answers and exclusion rules, pre-publication consistency check against that entity's own published history in the register). £349/month Group (up to 10 qualifying entities, consolidated filing calendar, one settings profile inherited across entities). £899/month Group Plus (unlimited entities, API upload, white-label pack for a group shared-service centre). RATIONALE: 3,762 of the 6,340 companies that filed in 2026 filed two or more reports, so per-entity-per-period is where the value actually scales — a group with eight qualifying subsidiaries produces sixteen statutory reports a year plus eight directors' report blocks. HONEST ANCHOR PROBLEM: there is no verified competitor price to anchor against. Forvis Mazars is quote-only; no dedicated SaaS with a published price was found. The anchor is therefore the alternative cost — a controller's two-to-five days per entity per period of ledger extraction and Excel reconciliation, plus the reg 8 exposure the corpus shows 27.2% of filers already carrying — not a fetched competitor number. That is a real weakness in the pricing case and is repeated in risks.
moat: Three layers, only one of which is genuinely hard to copy. (1) THE CALCULATION LINEAGE, WHICH IS THE REAL ASSET AND CANNOT BE BACKFILLED. Every period, for every entity, the product retains the invoice-level classification: which exclusion rule fired on which row, which date field served as receipt, which invoices were credit-noted out, how each speed band was populated, how the retention sums were built. From period two onward this makes the report a re-run rather than a re-derivation, and it is the only thing that can answer, months later, 'how was the figure we published in H1 arrived at' — the exact question reg 9 (knowingly or recklessly publishing misleading information) makes expensive. A competitor arriving in year three cannot reconstruct a customer's period-one lineage; the customer would have to re-derive it from archived ledgers. This is the same shape as the switching cost in any docketing product, but with criminal liability attached. (2) THE ENCODED SPEC. The reg 6 qualifying-contract tests, the exclusion list (financial services, residential occupiers, intra-entity payments, fully credit-noted invoices), the receipt-date rule that explicitly is not the software posting date, the count-versus-value distinction, and the two SI 2025/75 retention formulas are unglamorous, versioned, three-regime rule work that both ERP vendors have so far declined to complete. Versioning matters and is visible in the regulator's own data: the register stamps each report Regime-1, Regime-2 or Regime-3, and 2026 filings already span all three. (3) THE PUBLIC REGISTER AS A PRE-PUBLICATION CHECK. Because the corpus holds every figure the entity has ever published, the product can flag a step-change against its own filing history before publication, and benchmark it against the sector distribution — something no ERP report can do, because the ERP does not hold the public record. NOT A DEFENSIBLE TECHNOLOGY MOAT: the data is public, the spec is public, and any competent team could build the generator. The defence is the lineage archive, per-entity switching cost, and being first in a market with no incumbent — not secrecy.
risks: NOT YET PROVEN — THE BIGGEST GAP: nobody's price. I could not find a published consultant fee, a published SaaS price, or any dedicated tool in this category after four separate searches today. Forvis Mazars sells the service quote-only. So demand is inferred from three real signals (a Big-10 firm's service line, two ERP vendors funding recurring localisation work, and 27.2% measured non-compliance) but willingness to pay a specific number is unvalidated. The first validation step must be pricing, not building. SECOND RISK — PARTIAL BUNDLING HIT: Sage X3 and Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance both ship UK payment practices helper reports, and Microsoft demonstrably maintains its version (2026-05-12 doc, four release trains updated for the 2024 Regulations). Their own docs show they cover only the count-based statistics and stop short of the artifact, the value-based statistics and the construction retention block — but a single localisation release could close that gap, leaving us with pack assembly, the derivation workbook, benchmarking and the directors' report block. Mitigation is positioning as the last mile that consumes the ERP's own helper export as an input, not as its replacement. THIRD — BOUNDED TAM: 10,235 companies have ever filed; 6,340 filed in 2026. This is a finite market of roughly ten thousand buyers, not a long tail. Revenue must come from per-entity-per-period pricing and group expansion, and the ceiling should be modelled honestly before building. FOURTH — MY 27.2% LATE FIGURE IS AN UPPER BOUND: it is Filing date minus End date from the register, and does not account for adjusted reporting periods that DBT permits for non-standard or changed financial years, nor for a company's first year. It must be re-derived against DBT's own deadline calculator before it appears in any marketing copy, and until then it is an internal signal only. FIFTH — GARBAGE IN: if the customer's export has no true invoice-receipt date, the average-days statistic is wrong no matter how good the arithmetic — Microsoft's own documentation shows firms commonly default the receive date to the invoice date. The product must surface which field it used on the face of every pack rather than quietly substituting, or it becomes an accuracy liability under reg 9. SIXTH — REG 9 DISCIPLINE IS A PRODUCT CONSTRAINT, NOT A DISCLAIMER: the product can never present a figure as authoritative or as a compliance guarantee, and can never claim a customer will pass or fail a PPN 018 selection stage. It shows arithmetic, lineage and the published threshold; the director decides and signs. SEVENTH — GOVERNMENT COULD ADD A CSV UPLOAD to the publish service, deleting the keying friction (though not the calculation, the exclusions or the lineage). EIGHTH — the regime's statutory expiry is 6 April 2031 (SI 2024/444) with a review point pushed to 6 April 2029, so the obligation has a legislated horizon that must be watched.
